subject: Christmas Light Pollution
comment: Dear Council Member Dugan, You and I have spoken about light pollution in the past and I'm hoping that you might initiate a council discussion with the aim toward developing legislation in its regard and specifically "Christmas" lights. Wherein, more and more people are having permanent "Christmas" lights installed and, apparently, feeling compelled to entertain themselves and the rest of us with obnoxious options from their phone apps such as changing color, simulating movement and too often looking like a cheap motel, I believe it's time for some codified limitations. I completely understand not wanting to climb a ladder before and after the holidays to install and remove such lights so I'm not against the permanent installation. However, too often I see them in use well after the holiday season. My next-door neighbor, for example, uses her "Christmas" lights 365 days a year. A few other neighbors use tasteful static lights at 2,700K but others too often have theirs set at 5,000K which is glaringly garish. The Salt Lake City Clark Planetarium's Utah Dark Skies link suggests turning off lights when not needed and using shields to direct the light downward. https://www.saltlakecounty.gov/clark-planetarium/utah-dark-skies/ Salt Lake City's 21A.24.010: GENERAL PROVISIONS K states: Lighting: On site lighting shall be located, directed or designed in such a manner as to contain and direct light and glare only to the property on which it is located. My neighbor breaks this in spades and to me it's no different than playing loud music that I would hear inside my home. Park City has the following lighting ordinance which I applaud: Within Park City Limits (84060 zip code): Seasonal lights that do not cause light to spill out unnecessarily or interfere with the reasonable use and enjoyment of property are permitted from November 1 through March 1. Residential seasonal lights must be turned off by 11:00 p.m. I see no reason for people to leave their "Christmas" lights on all night long. Young children are hopefully in bed by 10:00 PM so I wonder whom these owners think is their target audience?Why the need to simulate movement and or color change and why add to light pollution when most people are in bed? And doesn't the year-round use diminish their impact of celebrating the holidays? Will every house, keeping up with the Jones, use them eventually thereby making every neighborhood look like the Vegas Strip? I believe the following limits, similar to the Park City ordinance, should be implemented for residential neighborhoods: - Off by 11:00 PM (exception for Christmas Eve?) - No color morphing or movement stimulation other than during the holiday season November 1st though January 31st - Year-round static use no more than 3,000K (I'd prefer the warmer -- and more tasteful -- 2,700K) Thanks for your attention and I'll keep my fingers crossed. I'd also like to have a discussion regarding residential speeding but that's for another day! Cheers, Ray Morrison

subject: Email
comment: Dear Councilmember Lopez Chavez, My name is Daniel Punt, and I am a homeowner and District 4 constituent living at REDACTED. I am writing to respectfully request your support in re-evaluating Salt Lake City's prohibition on artificial turf in front and corner side yards. I was surprised to recently learn that artificial turf is outright prohibited under Salt Lake City Ordinance 21A.48.080.B.4, which bars artificial turf in any location where landscaping is regulated by the City. I strongly support Salt Lake City's environmental and neighborhood goals, particularly in District 4, where we balance historic character, density, and sustainability. That said, given our high-desert climate, persistent drought conditions, and the urgent need to conserve water to protect resources such as the Great Salt Lake, I believe it is worth reassessing whether this policy still reflects today's conservation priorities. Outdoor irrigation represents a significant share of residential water use, and artificial turf—when used thoughtfully and in limited applications—can materially reduce water demand. Many water-stressed cities in the Southwest have moved toward incentive-based or flexible approaches rather than outright bans. In parts of the Phoenix metropolitan area, for example, cities encourage homeowners to replace water-intensive lawns with low-water alternatives through rebate programs, recognizing the need to adapt landscaping policies to modern water realities. As my District 4 representative, I respectfully ask whether you would consider supporting a discussion or review of this ordinance, including the possibility of pilot programs, conditional allowances, or other conservation-oriented updates. I would also appreciate any guidance on what steps I, or other District 4 residents, can take to help build thoughtful, community-supported momentum around potential policy change. Thank you for your time and for your service to our district and city. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this further. Sincerely, Daniel Punt

subject: No Camping Ordinance and Crime Technology Issues
comment: Dear Council Members, I have resided in Dan Dugan's district for decades and we developed, own and operate 283 apartment units across 3 projects in the heart of Sugar House (Sarah Young District) and at 315 West Pierpoint Ave downtown (Eva Lopez District). We have hundreds of residents that call these urban neighborhoods home, and we continue to be very concerned about public safety and crime in these neighborhoods.. I am writing to urge you to complete the drafting of the new ordinance regarding the definition of illegal "Camping" on public property in such a way that the police can do their job and remove illegal campers. The current ordinance is ineffective because it apparently requires that a structure be erected in order to be defined as "camping". There are many "camping" situations where the parties have household items, blankets, sleeping bags, and everything else spread around the park - essentially they have set up "camp" yet they are not technically considered as campers. This has to change, because it is facilitating illegal camping in parks and public areas. If it "walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck. Please fix the definition of camping. Another part of the ordinance rewrite which is critical is adding language that explicitly prohibits Recreational Vehicles "RVs" from "camping" by parking on the street. The current ordinance is unworkable because it simply limits the time an RV can park on the street and the RV Campers game the system by moving around the neighborhood for weeks and months effectively "camping" and staying within the prescribed time limits yet not leaving the neighborhood. Essentially these campers have been winning the game of cat and mouse with the police. You might say, oh well the RV campers are not doing any harm. To the contrary they bring a very dangerous element to the neighborhood. Just a month ago, on 2150 S Lincoln in Sugar House, a fatality resulted from an altercation over drugs that centered in an illegally parked RV that had been a menace to this neighborhood for many months. During that time period we made over 10 incident reports with photos to SLC parking enforcement. For the most part the parking enforcement would follow through and issue notices, mark tires etc. and the RV camper would just move around the corner. This went on for months and months with a number of incidents where the RV camper threatened us for taking photos of his illegal activity. We believe he was operating a drug dealing business out of the RV for many months. It all came to an end when his drug creditor shot him to death a month ago. This is of great concern to us as it occurred one half block from our project with 200 residents that are close to harm's way. This simply has to stop and again, it is an ordinance problem. Please clarify the ordinance such that RV Campers cannot use the streets of this city as an RV Campground. Make no mistake - there is a high correlation between "homeless" RV Campers and violent and deadly crime. It must stop and we must reclaim our neighborhoods. Another area of concern is helping the police use technology to prevent and fight crime. A recent incident on Pierpoint avenue involved assailants firing 6 shots at police officers. They fled without the police being able to see their license plates. There is technology called license plate readers that could have read the plates and a drone could have followed the vehicle but the police don't have the equipment. I was very disappointed to see on the news that the City Council voted to "defer" a $200,000 federal grant for license plate readers that would have put this equipment in the police's hands to save lives in our city. The "deferral" appeared to be based on some misguided politically correct views about immigration enforcement using the plate readers. Very misguided and sad that the council would put public safety as a low priority to political considerations. In summary, please rewrite the No Camping ordinance to broaden the definition of camping and to explicitly include RV Campers in the prohibition. Please fund technology equipment that will enable the police to prevent and fight crime, and please restore Public Safety as the top priority of this city. John Gardiner

subject: Evidence for Tonight's Meeting / SLCPU Zoning Misclassification
comment: Dear Council Member Puy, I am writing to provide you with a Memo of Opposition and technical exhibits regarding the Salt Lake City Public Utilities (SLCPU) project currently slated to begin this month at 1020 W. Pierpont Avenue. I will be attending tonight's Council meeting to speak on this matter, but I wanted to ensure you had the technical context beforehand, as this project involves what we believe is a significant zoning misclassification. Specifically, our research reveals that the City is permitting an active industrial bio-chemical wastewater treatment reactor as a simple "building or structure." This allows the Department to bypass the proper zoning reviews and environmental buffers required for such a facility—despite the fact that this reactor is being placed within 75 feet of single-family residences. While we appreciate the brief pause SLCPU granted, their recent actions suggest the "public engagement" process is largely performative. SLCPU claims to be listening to our concerns by holding another community meeting this Thursday; however, their most recent communication proves otherwise by stating that the project is still scheduled to commence this month. A one-to-two-week delay is a hollow gesture that is insufficient to address the identified procedural gaps. Most notably, there has been no time for necessary neighborhood or environmental impact modeling—such as odor or noise studies—and we still have not received a response to our formal GRAMA request regarding this project. We are requesting that the Council support a formal stay until a proper land-use review is conducted for a facility of this industrial scale and proximity. I have attached the Memo for your review and will have physical copies for the Council at tonight's meeting. Thank you for your time and for your representation of our community. Sincerely, Alex Ward

subject: Council Meeting Comment
comment: RE: 3 opportunities for SLC Council and SLC Mayor to better protect constitutional and human rights Executive Summary As our immigrant communities face increased fear and uncertainty, we have both the capability and the responsibility to further protect the constitutional and human rights of SLC businesses and residents. This memorandum outlines two key ways in which SLCPD can help decrease the fear in the community and increase the possibility of their rights being respected during and after encounters with federal ICE, HSI or equivalent agents. I also share Aurora, Colorado's latest resolution (see pp364) opposing unlawful and overreaching federal immigration enforcement actions as an example for Salt Lake City Council members to consider. In these unprecedented times, it is imperative to both serve the community and—wherever possible—preserve democracy, the rule of law, and individual rights. Background A January 2025 Federal Immigration enforcement action at Millcreek Much like the late January 2025 ICE incident where an ICE agent signed a false statement accusing a gentleman of trying to side-swipe his car and hit him, I have knowledge of multiple individuals who have more recently been threatened with similar false Federal charges. While I understand the limited role a local police department can occupy when Federal agents are on scene, I believe there are at least two areas where more can be done, in addition to the current verification of Federal agents that SLCPD can provide if someone calls 911 when masked, armed men refuse to identify themselves. Recommendation: Assigning a case number/opening an investigation in instances like the January 2025 Millcreek one where Federal agents are suspected or proven to have lied, targeted individuals need access to security cam footage from nearby businesses or homes to prove their innocence. Most businesses will only release this footage if requested by a police department. Whether assigning a case number, opening an investigation, or simply giving the targeted individual a business card to share with their lawyer, SLCPD can—by facilitating and acquiring security cam footage—increase transparency, verify or debunk the claims of Federal ICE agents, and ensure targeted residents and business owners are treated with respect according to the rule of law. Recommendation: Timing and thoroughness of verification SLCPD is already able to reduce fear in the community by responding to 911 calls where federal agents refuse to show identification or warrants, making it impossible for targeted individuals to know if they're being legally detained or unlawfully assaulted and kidnapped. While they cannot interfere with a federal agent, they should help document when those federal agents violate the Constitutional rights of Salt Lake City residents. Witnessing and documenting ICE encounters has been shown to increase the likelihood that rights will be respected, whether or not anyone is detained. The average ICE encounter lasts less than 10-15 minutes. With the existing local precedent that at least one ICE agent has lied in a sworn statement and endangered the rights of a US Citizen, the need for volunteer or legal observers to be on scene in real time is paramount. As local volunteers learn of active ICE encounters, we quickly rush to the scene to legally observe and document ICE activity to preserve the rights of targeted individuals without interfering with federal agents. Anything that increases the time it takes for an ICE incident to be completed improves the chances that a volunteer observer can arrive on scene to remind the targeted individual of their Constitutional rights, contact their legal representation, and legally document the encounter for rights violations. It would be helpful to know how SLCPD verifies the legitimacy of federal agents, how thorough the verification process is, and how long it takes, on average. Recommendation: SLC Council resolution opposing unlawful and overreaching federal immigration enforcement actions I respectfully request the SLC Council consider an urgent resolution similar to one shared by Aurora, CO (see pp364) denouncing the recent, illegal escalation by federal ICE agents and officials. These escalations have further eroded our democracy, violated Constitutional rights, and needlessly taken the life of Renee Nicole Good, among others. Conclusion I appreciate the sensitivity of this matter and the position SLCPD and SLC elected officials are in, given the volatility and complexity of today's political environment. This matter is fundamentally about preserving the individual and Constitutional rights of SLC businesses and residents—part of the sworn duty of public servants. I believe the recommendations are simple, low-cost, and have the potential to improve the lives of all SLC residents across the board. Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to speak further about any of these ideas at your convenience.

subject: Please Oppose Rezoning of Northpoint Wetlands
comment: Council Member Dugan, I'm writing as a District 6 resident to urge you to oppose the proposed rezoning of 80 acres of designated Natural Open Space in the Northpoint community to industrial use. The City's recently adopted Northpoint Small Area Plan, created through years of community engagement, clearly identifies this land as protected Natural Open Space. Changing that designation now would undermine the planning process and permanently eliminate one of the last large wetland playas in the area. At a time when the Great Salt Lake is shrinking, these wetlands are essential. subject: Great Salt Lake wetlands
comment: To the Salt Lake City Council, My name is James Miska, and I am a local resident, homeowner, and small business owner in the tourism industry, here in Salt Lake City. I am writing because I am against the proposal of upzoning of 80 acres of Great Salt Lake wetlands in the Northpoint area. The land is now zoned as agricultural, and in previous planning documents, the city has said the land should be preserved as open space and wetlands. Therefore, the city should deny the proposal to upzone it, plain and simple. The issue is on its way to making it to your agenda for a future City Council meeting, so I wanted to get this comment in writing to you now. As you may be aware, on Jan. 14th, 2026, the SLC Planning Commission voted unanimously to deny the proposals in question (PLNPCM2025-00613 and PLNPCM2025-00614). I request that you allow City Council unanimously act in accordance with this clear opinion of the Planning Commission as concerns this matter. At a time when the Great Salt Lake is shrinking before our eyes, this rezoning would permanently erase approximately 80 acres of irreplaceable wetland playa—lands that quietly sustain the lake, shelter wildlife, and protect our communities. These wetlands are not empty or expendable. They are living, breathing parts of the Great Salt Lake ecosystem, and once they are gone, they are gone forever. The proposed rezoning would destroy one of the last large remaining wetland playas in the Northpoint area, harming adjacent wetlands and duck clubs and bringing increased diesel truck traffic, air pollution, contaminated runoff, noise, and light pollution. These impacts would further burden surrounding communities and an area the City has already identified as environmentally fragile. The City's recently adopted Northpoint Small Area Plan reflects years of community engagement and clearly designates this land as Natural Open Space, intended to remain undeveloped. The Plan identifies wetlands and sensitive lands as least suitable for development and directs industrial uses away from environmentally constrained areas. I am also deeply concerned by the incomplete public input process. The initial 45-day Public Input Notice described this request only as a rezoning from AG-2 to M-1 and failed to disclose that the property is designated as Natural Open Space and wetlands in the adopted General Plan—or that amending the General Plan would be required. This critical information was later included in the Planning Commission notice, confirming that it is material. The omission denied the public a meaningful opportunity to provide informed input. Approving these proposals would reflect poorly on the institution of our local government. For all these reasons, please deny the proposals PLNPCM2025-00613 and PLNPCM2025-00614 I would like a response to this message. Thank you, James Miska

subject: SLCDPU's planned January 12th construction of a 30-foot industrial reactor vessel
comment: Dear City Council Members: We are writing to you ahead of today's 4:00 PM Community Town Hall to express our grave concerns regarding the SLCDPU's planned January 12th construction of a 30-foot industrial reactor vessel ("BioTower") at 1020 W Pierpont Ave (Permit BLD2025-02186). According to the City's own engineering specifications, this is not a standard utility structure, but a high-capacity industrial system designed for continuous 24/7 processing. We have formally requested an Executive Stay from the Mayor's office to ensure this project does not proceed while the Council is in the middle of finalizing Petitions PLNPCM2024-01352 and PLNPCM2024-01357. We ask the Council to consider the following three points: 1. Legislative Clarification: We urge you to ensure that these pending petitions include explicit language prohibiting "BioTowers" and similar installations in residential zones. Clarifying these standards now will provide much-needed certainty for both the city and its residents, ensuring that industrial processes are never again proposed for placement in a residential backyard. 2. Geographic Inequity: This would be the first industrial BioTower ever sited in a residential neighborhood in Salt Lake City. The only other existing BioTowers are in strictly industrial areas on the West Side. Despite holding 60% of the city's population, the East Side remains entirely BioTower-free. 3. Environmental Health: According to the EPA's EJScreen tool, Poplar Grove already ranks in the 96th percentile for Diesel Particulate Matter (soot) and the 99th percentile nationally for proximity to hazardous waste facilities. Placing an industrial chemical exhaust system ~80 feet from residential front doors is an undue cumulative burden on a neighborhood that is already at its breaking point. We were notified by Council Member Puy this past Friday that he is out of the country and will not be attending today's meeting. While he has been aware of this situation since December 22nd, his current absence during this critical window means we must look to the full Council to provide the legislative oversight needed to protect our community. We invite you to join us at 1020 W Pierpont Ave today at 4:00 PM. We want to give you the opportunity to see, firsthand, just how extreme the proximity of this industrial reactor vessel will be to the front doors of our families' homes. Thank you for your time and for protecting the integrity of the Council's legislative work. Sincerely, Alex Ward on behalf of the Poplar Grove Residents

subject: Comments on parking requirements, transportation safety, CIP
comment: Hi Erika, I appreciated your attendance and Q&A at the Central City Neighborhood Council this wednesday, despite representing only a small portion of our neighborhood! I wanted to reach out with some follow up thoughts following my question on transportation safety. I'm happy to chat sometime on any of the topics if you'd like. Minimum Parking Requirements This is a tough subject, because the wording and understanding for the public is very important. The city requires a minimum amount of off-street parking everywhere except within a set short distance of TRAX. These mandates require a significant expense to construction, degrade our environment by converting green space to pavement, and add driveways, which leads to decreased safety and ironically, a reduction in on-street parking (no parking in front of or within 5 ft of a driveway). For these reasons, I believe the city should not require off-street parking city-wide. To be clear, this only impacts the city requirement for off-street parking, developers can still choose to build parking, and are often forced to through financing (see the 144 South Apartments project). I just want to have the choice to, say, have a garden instead of a parking spot (mind you I'd be forced to have one and pay for it even though I don't own a car!) Many consider new townhomes to be ugly, and that is in no small part because they're surrounded by parking access, and costs are driven up by 1/3 of the building being a garage. It also bothers me that the wonderful housing I see in our older neighborhoods would be illegal to build today. Reform here needs to be focused on removing the requirement, not "removing parking", as many are already confused from previous efforts as well as misinformation that the city is physically removing parking. Safety I'm glad to hear that you support safety measures. These measures impact everyone. While there's a lot of focus on vulnerable road users, drivers really benefit the most by these measures which reduce crashes and crash severity. I think there is a silent majority out there that would much rather drive safely, but feel pressured by other drivers to drive more aggressively, or the street design promotes bad driving behavior. Safety is inevitably linked to on-street parking, and unfortunately, everyone wants to park in front of their destination and experience parking pressures everyday such that this desire overpowers the more infrequent but much more impactful safety needs. I think there is in part a cultural shift here needed - it's okay not to park in front of your destination if you don't need to, and that streets that are meant to move people (traffic streets) should prioritize the safe movement of people before considering on-street parking. Redesignating a shoulder on a traffic street for a bike lane when there's more parking around the corner should be a no-brainer. In a lot of cases we have the space to have both, but that usually requires longer-term, more expensive projects. Central Ninth is a good example that shows that even though most of the street space is still dedicated to cars (two lanes, two diagonal parking lanes, and central walkway access to parking), people still demand more parking. Meanwhile pedestrians and cyclists often share space because the sidewalk on the 9 Line is too small. A practical solution is to guide drivers to existing lots and garages instead of everyone competing for limited on street parking, not because they need it but because there's a lack of awareness of other options. This way we can redirect our efforts to saving lives instead of battling over a parking spot. With that said, we can make other improvements that don't touch parking, like protected intersections, better lighting, traffic calming, and etc. I also want to note terminology here as well, particularly around the topic of traffic calming - I think saying "slowing traffic" is not the move, instead "stopping speeders" should resonate better when speaking with residents. Slowing traffic implies slower travel times, but really travel time is regulated more by traffic signals. Stopping speeders better implies that it's difficult to go significantly over the speed limit - and that's what traffic calming does! CIP Applications - I brought up a CIP application for 700 South in Salt Lake City, but I have also submitted an application in your district, for improved crossings on 1700 South. The application targets currently unsignalized intersections along the street that are designated neighborhood byways in the city's master plan. As someone who frequently gets around by bike in the city, 1700 South is one of the most obvious gaps in safe infrastructure, and this application is a great start to at least make it easier to cross the street. Improvements would include curb extensions and flashing beacons, though we don't focus on traffic calming along 1700 South due to 2025's SB195 bill, which scrutinizes traffic calming on non-residential streets. I would, however, love to see future efforts to make 1700 South safer. Note that city transportation had an opportunity to update the paint striping recently but it got caught up in the SB195 debacle last year, and I hope that's revisited. I'll also add that between my two CIP applications, they're focused on building neighborhood byways. These are residential streets that are already low traffic, but just need to have minor traffic calming within the route and mostly the safe crossings of major streets. These bode well with the public, because they typically remove little if any parking and focus on streets that only residents live on, so there's no worry about needing to perform traffic studies. The City is slowly chipping away at a network of neighborhood byways, but they're currently only funded by one-off opportunities like CIPs, thus it's vital to fund work each year. Thank you for taking the time to read my comments! Troy

subject: Opposition to name change of Harvey Milk Blvd.
comment: I am a Salt Lake County resident with strong ties to Salt Lake City and writing to express my strong opposition and outrage to the proposal to rename Harvey Milk Boulevard. If the intent were truly to honor another individual, there are numerous unnamed streets or new developments where that could be done. Choosing instead to replace an existing honorary designation is not neutral. It is a symbolic act, and symbols matter. This proposal does not add to our shared history—it attempts to overwrite it. Harvey Milk Boulevard represents more than a name. It stands for visibility, dignity, and the hard-won recognition of LGBTQ+ people who were historically and currently still are excluded, silenced, or erased. To single out this street for replacement sends a clear message that such recognition is provisional and can be revoked for political reasons. Equally concerning is the precedent this sets. Street naming has long been a matter of local governance. State-level intervention in this process undermines local control and disregards the voices of the residents who live, work, and conduct business in this community. This issue is not about partisan preference. It is about whether we choose coexistence over erasure, and whether our government uses its authority to unify or to provoke. Salt Lake City is capable of honoring multiple histories without diminishing any of them. I hope you will consider not just the policy implications of this proposal but the message it sends to those who rely on public symbols to know they belong. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Karen Stagnaro Salt Lake County resident

subject: Concerns Regarding ICE Detention Facilities in Salt Lake City
comment: Subject: Concerns Regarding ICE Detention Facilities in Salt Lake City To the Members of the Salt Lake City Council, I am writing to urge the Council to consider and pass an emergency ordinance requiring a conditional use permit for ICE detention facilities in Salt Lake City. Such a measure would provide the City Council and Planning Commission with the legal authority to prevent the construction and operation of detention facilities that pose serious ethical, legal, and humanitarian concerns. ICE detention facilities have a well-documented history of inhumane conditions, including failures to provide adequate food, medical care, and basic protections for those detained. Reports have shown that ICE has at times stopped paying for detainee medical care even as detention populations increased, placing lives at risk. More recently, ICE has begun detaining children in these facilities, escalating these concerns into clear human rights violations through the neglect and mistreatment of both children and adults. There are also deeply troubling cases in which U.S. citizens—including children—have been detained and transported out of state, separating them from their families, communities, and access to legal counsel. Salt Lake City has a responsibility to protect its residents and uphold fundamental human rights. Allowing the expansion or operation of ICE detention facilities within city limits runs counter to those values and exposes the community to unnecessary harm and liability. I urge the Council to take decisive action to prevent these facilities from operating in Salt Lake City and to stand firmly in defense of human dignity, due process, and community safety. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Emma Baker Bountiful, UT

subject: Keep the MU-8 Zoning east of St. Marks Cathedral
comment: The City Council should keep the current MU-8 zoning for the property at 265 East 100 South for three reasons. First, the proposal to change the property to D-1 to accommodate the developer's quest to build a higher building than the MU-8 zoning allows goes against the long-term City policy of having firm boundaries define the downtown. The City's plans consistently have set the downtown's eastern boundary at roughly 250 East Street to keep the downtown from bleeding eastward into residential areas. A 1988 Regional/Urban Design Assistance Team study advised the City to "develop a new 'Urban Neighborhood" zoning classification for the area bounded by a mid-block line between 200 East and 300 East to provide for "urban neighborhoods" to envelop the commercial core and make the downtown the focal point of high-quality, high-density development and design. It's the reason the downtown is what it is today. It is the result of the study's advice that, "the community will only succeed in redeveloping downtown if the major stakeholders (including the City, LDS Church, developers, and the business community, and neighborhoods) can support a single vision and strategy for downtown and pursue it consistently over a period of time." Second, the MU-8 zoning has not had enough time for the City to see whether the zoning will work. The Council adopted the zoning in 2025. Why not see what the zoning will accomplish instead of immediately responding to a developer's pleading of special case? The developer must have known what the City's plans were to implement the MU-8 zone. Why seek to change it? The City Council staff report raises a similar issue. According to the report, "It is important to note that if the zoning map amendment is adopted by the Council there is no guarantee the proposed development will be constructed. The property could be redeveloped with any use allowed within the zone or sold to another party. The Council is only being asked to consider rezoning the property. Because zoning of a property can outlast the life of a building, any rezoning application should be considered on the merits of changing the zoning of that property, not simply based on a potential project." (Staff Report, Page 3.) The City faced a similar issue with the proposed residential building at the corner of 1100 East and 2100 South and stayed with the existing zoning. Sugar House is going to get a much, much better building that fits into the fabric of that area because of the City's decision to adhere to existing plans. Third, the Sugar House residential building and the earlier proposal to build a gas station and convenience store by Sugar House Park raise another point. Do the proposed buildings, even if the main structure is capped at 225 feet, fit into the neighborhood? Except for the law offices at the corner of 200 East 100 South, the buildings along 100 South are low-key condominiums and apartment buildings sharing space with neighborhood businesses - and St. Marks Cathedral. Is that a neighborhood that warrants an edifice? Like the original building proposed in Sugar House, the proposed building in the proposed D-1 zone is an underwhelming design that will overwhelm the existing neighborhood. The design for the building that complies with the MU-8 zoning shown in the transmittal and staff report portrays a better structure that fits into the neighborhood.

subject: Inquiry regarding Call 2 Haul eligibility and policy equity
comment: Dear SLC Sustainability Department and City Council Members, I am writing to request a policy update to the Call 2 Haul program that would extend eligibility to residents in multi-family buildings. I am a homeowner at REDACTED. Our building houses 48 families on a footprint equivalent to roughly six suburban lots. Despite this being the exact model of "smart growth" the city promotes, we are currently excluded from the Call 2 Haul program due to its restriction to properties with 1–4 units. I have bulk items ready for disposal and would prefer to utilize a city-sanctioned program. I am seeking either a policy update to include multi-family properties or guidance on a service buy-in option for homeowners in buildings like mine. I understand this limitation may stem from legacy zoning classifications, but I believe it creates an unintended disparity that runs counter to the city's sustainability goals. Residents in Downtown, Central City, Sugar House, and the Granary District amongst many other areas are choosing high-density living to reduce their environmental footprint. However, current eligibility rules inadvertently penalize this choice by denying us access to the diversion services our property taxes help fund. Expanding the program to include multi-family buildings would be consistent with the city's goals for three reasons: Logistical Efficiency: Our building has a centralized dumpster and loading zone. Servicing 48 households at one stop is objectively more carbon-efficient than a city truck traveling to 48 separate suburban driveways. Sustainability Logic: Forcing high-density residents—many of whom do not own large vehicles—to hire private, landfill-bound haulers contradicts the city's goals of reducing emissions and preventing illegal dumping in urban areas. Fiscal Equity: High-density developments contribute significantly more property tax per acre to the General Fund than single-family neighborhoods. We should have equitable access to municipal services, regardless of outdated billing classifications. Could you please direct me to the individual responsible for Call 2 Haul eligibility policy? I would also appreciate understanding the timeline for reviewing these boundaries to better serve the city's growing high-density neighborhoods. Thank you for your time and consideration. Best regards, Justin Justin Kani

subject: Concerns Regarding ICE Facilities in SLC
comment: To the Salt Lake City Council, I am writing to urge the Council to adopt an emergency ordinance requiring a conditional use permit for any ICE detention facility within Salt Lake City. Doing so would provide the Council and the Planning Commission with the legal authority to prevent the construction and operation of detention facilities that pose serious humanitarian and public safety concerns. ICE detention facilities have a well-documented record of abuse and neglect, including failures to provide adequate medical care, nutrition, and basic human dignity to those in custody. These are not isolated incidents, but systemic problems that have been repeatedly documented by journalists and watchdog organizations. When the state knowingly allows such facilities to operate, it becomes complicit in that harm. The situation becomes even more alarming given that ICE has begun detaining children in these facilities. The detention of children under conditions marked by neglect and trauma constitutes a grave human rights violation. Additionally, these facilities enable U.S. citizens—including children—to be transported out of state, separated from their communities, families, and legal representation. That should concern every resident of this city, regardless of political affiliation. Salt Lake City has long positioned itself as a place that values human dignity, due process, and the safety of its residents. The City Council has both the authority and the responsibility to act when federal practices threaten those values within city limits. Requiring a conditional use permit is a necessary and reasonable step to protect our community from becoming a site of documented abuse and injustice. I urge you to take swift action and pass this emergency ordinance. Thank you for your time and for your service to our city. Sincerely, Kaitlyn Rowbotham Sandy, 84092

subject: Winter water rates and water conservation - D2
comment: Hello, Alejandro, Like everyone, we are very concerned about water conservation. Our SLC policy of basing summer water rates on winter consumption is generally a good policy. However, with the lack of snow, our trees are suffering and require winter water, and trees take a lot! I don't want my trees to die. subject: ICE Out Protest
comment: Hello Council Member Dugan, My name is Max, and I am currently a senior at Judge Memorial Catholic High School. I will be graduating in May and moving into the University of Utah dorms this August to begin a four-year degree. My purpose in writing today is to reach out to local leaders about concerns I believe affect people across political lines. There are two main issues I would like to focus on: ICE and political representation. I am fully aware that ICE has been responsible for the deaths of dozens of non-citizens and, more recently, two American citizens in Minneapolis. I do not want to see a situation like this reach Utah. I firmly believe that violence should never be tolerated, let alone excused. At the same time, I do not believe ICE should be abolished. In concept, ICE serves an important purpose and can be useful. My concern is with how it is currently being used — often functioning as a policing force that must follow federal directives while facing very few consequences. Because of this, I believe ICE should be relocated back to the border and refocused on border protection rather than interior enforcement. My second concern relates to political representation, which I believe plays a major role in how issues like this become so polarized. As humans, we naturally label things to better understand them, but political labeling has gone too far. We often agree on nearly everything except one issue, yet that single disagreement can make cooperation feel impossible. I believe people should be able to vote for who they genuinely support, rather than feeling pressured to choose between the two major parties. To help explain this concern, I would like to compare two elections: 1912 and 2012. Both resulted in Democratic victories, but the range of political choice available to voters differed greatly. In 1912, the Progressive Party received 27% of the vote, placing second, while Republicans received 23%. Although Democrats won decisively in the Electoral College with 435 votes, those numbers do not fully reflect voter support across parties. When comparing electoral votes to popular votes, Democrats in 1912 received roughly one electoral vote per 14,540 popular votes, while the Progressive Party received one per 46,800. Even when applying the same comparison to the 2012 election approximately 1:198,000 and 1:296,000 a noticeable imbalance still exists. The Electoral College often encourages campaigns to focus on winning individual states rather than representing the country as a whole. While it was originally intended to balance the power of less populous states with more populous ones, assigning electoral votes largely based on population can have the opposite effect. Instead of creating fairness, it can amplify disparities and shift attention away from broader national electorate. I am not writing to promote one party or ideology over another. Rather, I hope to better understand how local leaders view these issues and whether there is room for policies that encourage accountability, cooperation, and broader representation. I appreciate you taking the time to read this and consider the perspective of a young voter who wants to stay engaged in our community. Sincerely, Max This email reflects my own views and was written by me, with some assistance from AI to improve organization and clarity, for I am not a great writer but a great thinker.

subject: Request for Review of Digital Lending Costs and Sustainability
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Library Board, City Council, and Library CEO, I am writing to share concerns about the long term sustainability and financial impact of the current e book lending model used by Salt Lake City's public libraries. As you are aware, libraries do not own most e books and digital audiobooks. Instead, they must license them at prices significantly higher than the consumer market rate, often with strict limits on the number of loans or required re-purchasing after a set number of checkouts. These licensing structures place a substantial and recurring financial burden on public libraries and, ultimately, on taxpayers and renters who indirectly bear these costs. My concerns include: 1. High Costs for E Book Licensing Publishers typically charge libraries many times the consumer price for a single digital title, often requiring renewal after only a few dozen loans. This creates a situation where popular books can cost far more than physical copies we would own permanently. 2. Reduced Support for Authors Because so much funding is directed toward expensive short term licenses, less remains for building long term collections—including physical books that can support a broader range of authors over time. 3. Impact on Local Community Resources Salt Lake City has wonderful physical library spaces that serve as important "third places" for learning, community gathering, and local employment. Heavy investment in digital rentals risks shifting funds away from maintaining and expanding these community assets. 4. Sustainability Concerns The current model encourages a kind of "fast fashion" approach to reading—rapid consumption of high demand digital titles that are expensive and fleeting—rather than building a durable, locally owned collection. There are thousands of outstanding works, including many in the public domain, that could be preserved and shared permanently at minimal cost. 5. Accessibility Should Remain a Priority Digital materials are essential for patrons with disabilities, mobility limitations, or those who rely on assistive technologies. Ensuring continued access for these users is important. My concern is with the scale and cost of general digital lending, not the existence of accessibility driven services. _________________________________ My Request I respectfully ask that the city and library leadership: • Reevaluate the balance between digital and physical media spending • Consider capping non accessibility-based needed digital borrowing where possible • Prioritize investments in physical collections, local jobs, and public library spaces • Ensure that public funds are used in a sustainable manner that benefits the community long term My perspective comes from a desire to support the financial health of our library system and maintain the strong, community-oriented spaces that make Salt Lake City a great place to live. Thank you for your consideration and for everything you do to support literacy, learning, and community well being. Sincerely, Nelson Neuberger. Salt Lake City resident and homeowner.

subject: Concerns about Water Infrastructure Legislation
comment: I am reaching out to you with some concerns I have about HB 501 and how it will impact local governments and water providers, taking away local control and creating a new level of bureaucracy. HB 501's tax on all Utahns will be used to expand state government. This new bill at the Utah Legislature proposes a new tax on all water bills to fund Utah government and pay for gigantic water projects that could harm the Great Salt Lake and divert water out of the Colorado River. HB 501 would set a tax on municipal water rates and sewer bills to fund water development projects inside Utah state government. Utahns currently pay property taxes on their cars, housing, and businesses for water, they pay two different sales taxes for water, and now they would pay a new tax on all their water bills. The bill does not specify which water projects would receive these funds, but big water projects that are currently authorized and collecting sales tax funds include both the $3-4 billion proposed Bear River Development and $3-4 billion Lake Powell Pipeline. Smaller water projects could also be funded by these taxes. The tax would be determined by multiplying a percentage times the median income in any given water supplier's service area. This means that in communities like Salt Lake City, where the median income is significantly higher than household incomes in poorer communities, the working poor will be paying a disproportionately large amount compared to wealthy households on the east bench and upper avenues. Funds could be used for Bear River Development, a controversial water project that would be the death knell for the Great Salt Lake. Proposed Bear River Development would divert the Bear River to the lawns of the Wasatch Front upstream of the Great Salt Lake. Because the Bear River is the single largest source of water to the Great Salt Lake, proposed Bear River Development would lower lake levels dramatically, impacting air quality and wetland bird populations. All Utah residents will eventually pay this tax, but that doesn't mean they'll receive any water from the projects it funds. Worse yet, the biggest water wasters along the Wasatch Front — secondary water users — will not have to pay this tax. Furthermore, Utah's biggest water users — farmers — won't pay this tax either, except in their household water bills. Agriculture uses 80-85% of all the water used in Utah. The next House Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Environment Committee is scheduled for Wednesday February 11th at 2:00 PM. It's possible that the bill could be heard in committee at that time, where there is the opportunity for public comment in person or online. We are working on a calculator to determine the contribution each city would make under this bill and can send that to you soon, if you are interested in the financial impact this would have on your community and water utility. The bill can be found at https://le.utah.gov/~2026/bills/static/HB0501.html The problematic language language starts around line 611. Please reach out if you have any questions and pass this information on to anyone in your city. The Utah League of Cities and Towns is opposing this bill. Amy Wicks Northern Utah Program Manager Great Salt Lake Waterkeeper Utah Rivers Council Utah Rivers Council Northern Office

This is an urgent safety issue that we have come to the city and district with more than once in recent years. subject: Northpoint Upzone
comment: Dear Council Members, As you know, the Salt Lake Planning Commission voted to forward a negative recommendation to the Salt Lake City Council. I hope that when this issue comes up for a vote at the Council, you will consider voting against it. The 2023 Sackett ruling at the Supreme Court drastically changed the definition of wetlands, eliminating protections from ephemeral wetlands, important wetlands areas that are not always wet. While these areas may not always appear to be wetlands, they play an important role in natural ecosystems. At some point, this 80 acres was identified as wetlands, indicating it falls into the category of "ephemeral wetlands." Worldwide there is a 0.52% annual decline in wetland areas. According to the EPA, wetland area benefits include water storage and filtering, groundwater recharge and discharge, floodplain development, nutrient cycling and providing wildlife habitat. Trading preservation of one wetland area for another is not a good option as it results in net loss of overall wetland area. We need all the wetlands we can get, especially as we struggle to save the Great Salt Lake. Although this area is relatively small, it is one of many being impacted. Huge economic development projects, from Spanish Fork to Box Elder County, including the inland port, have already, and will continue to impact wetland areas. In the Northpoint Small Area plan, this parcel was to be preserved as open space. Other assurances, including truck traffic rerouting and buffers between industrial and residential, and industrial and natural space were promised. None of these have happened and this rural area is being sacrificed for the worst kinds of development. Why would any local small business want to locate here? I urge you to vote against this upzone and join Salt Lake County in adopting a resolution to protect wetland areas, public and private, along the shores of the Great Salt Lake. Respectfully, Katie Pappas Salt Lake City 84103

subject: Opposition to Extended Downtown (N. S. & W. Temple) Street Closures
comment: I strongly oppose this proposal. Closing major downtown corridors for up to eight months is excessive and unreasonable. North Temple, West Temple, and South Temple are essential arteries for residents, small businesses, transit riders, and daily commuters. An extended closure of this scale shifts the burden of a private event onto the broader public. Public safety can and should be addressed through targeted traffic control, limited-duration closures, and active management during peak times. An eight-month shutdown of key streets is not a balanced solution. Downtown businesses are still recovering and rely on predictable access. Residents deserve mobility and transparency. The City should not grant exclusive use of public right-of-way for such an extended period. This proposal goes too far and should not move forward in its current form.

subject: Constituent in support of HB381 S3 and related comments opposing SB242's anti-safe streets in SLC section Constituent in support of HB581 S3 and related comments opposing SB242's anti-safe streets in SLC section
comment: Dear Senator Plumb and fellow elected officials, As an e-bicycle must love our Electric Mobility Device Amendments, I am a constituent who owns two electric bicycles, a Riese and Muller cargo bike for bigger shopping errands and a Tern folding bike to get around town. These are in addition to my 4 other regular bicycles and my husband's collection of 6 more. We have always been a bike-ctl family thanks to living in historic East Central in Salt Lake City with good options besides driving thanks to being close to work, shopping, and UTA routes. That means we can afford to own a lot of bikes - nice ones. Bicycle and Electric Assist Bicycle Benefits A study in Scientific American revealed that cycling is the most energy-efficient mode of travel. "Humans aren't very efficient movers—until you put us on a bicycle, when we become some of the most energy-efficient land travelers in the animal kingdom." https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/e-human-on-a-bicycle-is-simple-the-most-efficient-forms-of-travel-in-the/ Plus, it's especially healthier, more fun, and pro-social. Except for the frequent fear factor on our many dangerous Utah and capital city streets. What is great about my electric bicycles? They extend my effective range, make starting up again at intersections more efficient, and reduce barriers like hills and wind. Plus did I mention fun? My cargo bike also gets a lot of positive comments out and around town - as a conservatively dressed woman of a certain age who is otherwise largely invisible I enjoy that. If you don't have an electric assist bicycle yet, I highly recommend test riding and online pre- I still ride my other bikes, but the e-bikes tend to get out more often these days. I assets at age 61 that's OK Better E-motorcycle regulation needed like in HB381 That said, I have been concerned about the proliferation of dangerous visiting throttle-only (non-pedal) pseudo-bicycles- little e-motorcycles. HB381 appropriately recognizes electric-assist pedal bicycles and throttle-only electric motorcycles as two very different categories and works to better address this. The forms and models of e-motorcycles have been changing rapidly and the laws have not kept up. It's not the fuel source; it's the propulsion and speed capabilities that make the biggest difference. Many of the reported injuries nationally are due to teens playing around on these more dangerous e-motors. Opposition to Helmet Laws for bicycles and electric bicycles (OK for e-motorcycles) I was concerned when it seemed that an under-21 helmet requirement could apply to all e-bikes for riders under 21; the bill summary isn't very clear. But in reading through HB381 S3 it looks like that is now revised 3" certain devices" so I am comfortable with that language. Studies show that helmet requirements for bicyclists can reduce head injuries to a limited extent but data shows that this may well be due to overall drop in cycling, not safer conditions for riders. This is not a good tradeoff when other things can reduce it "effectively If I never leave my house I will never be at risk of a crash or injury outdoors. That's not safety; that's being trapped. Helmet requirements may also stop some riders with fines even if they were riding safely, and this is often quite arbitrary. Minority and other disadvantaged riders may be more likely to be noticed by officers and subject to disproportionate enforcement; this is common with "jaywalking" (another very problematic category of violations). While I do support helmets as a smart choice for higher speed recreational riding and younger riders, in my opinion they should not be required by law. Yes, head injuries are a real risk from bad crashes. So are many other kinds of injuries bicyclists can't prevent. I also own several helmets but if I am just running errands on our better-designed streets like 200 and 300 South, I generally don't bother. At some point the responsibility must fall on riders, and on children's parents, to reduce personal choice unless appropriately. The need for Safe Streets By Design for Public Safety, Health, Economic Vitality, and Protection of Life To reduce systemic risks and also increase individual freedom of mobility, it is the responsibility of state and local governments to build and maintain safe, multimodal streets for all users. That is what generates the biggest safety benefit for all – including drivers – as shown by city after city, country after country, that actually do this. Far too many US and Utah civil engineers remain mired in out-of-date, dangerous street design models they were taught decades ago that have failed in both safety and efficient mobility in dense, complex city environments. Luckily, national guidelines such as NACTO https://nacto.org/ and even AASHTO are catching up. But local practices are too slow to change. The best cities in the world create safe urban environments by designing better and more complete street infrastructure or for pedestrians, cyclists, and riders alike. Most day-to day commuters and cyclists in these cities don't wear helmets, though many children do. I am getting old and impatient for safer streets for all. I fear I will never live to see the day Salt Lake City and other Utah cities level up to match the best cities in the country and world. Frankly, we are considering moving after retirement for this reason - we want to be able to age in place in a livable, active mobility, healthy community with clean air and safe streets. As someone who has donated so much personal time to community and volunteerism to improve our neighborhoods, city, and state, this is profoundly sad. Opposition to SB242's anti-safety anti-SLC dangerous language Especially now. The Legislature may make that even more impossible here in the capital city unless SB242 is amended. My recent visit to the Netherlands showed why safe streets by design works - they have focused for decades on safety by design: lower traffic speeds, separated and consistently designed street facilities including safe cycle networks, smart signaling, better transit. It was wonderful for all modes of travel - including having some of the most satisfied drivers in the world! Car traffic flows best when all the other modes are efficient and designed to have their own lanes - bicycle, sidewalk, transit, cars. Or compare the success of Oslo, Norway in Vision Zero and City livability but as compared to current conditions in Salt Lake City: https://thecityfix.com/blog/how-oslo-achieved-zero-pedestrian-and-bicycle-fatalities-and-how-others-can-apply-what-worked/ It's too many drivers and high speed, car-dependent, car-sewer car-filled streets and dangerous intersections that are creating the car traffic congestion and hazards. When people like me must bicycle in the car traffic lane because there is no bike lane, it is scary and also slows car traffic - not when I am in a bike lane! I experience this a lot on nearby streets 100 South, the west side of South Temple, 300 East, and more. As a driver, I am so frustrated when there are no bike lanes for the same reason. This is why a complete, connected network is so necessary. Car drivers get that - so should cyclists especially on our excessively wide streets. When I was a child, the majority of kids walked or bicycled to school. Now, that rate has plummeted and most kids get driven to school, trapping parents in the chase and impairing the health and well-being of children as well as creating a vicious cycle where the remaining kids who still try to walk or ride are threatened by all the car drivers. In the Netherlands, by contrast, most kids still ride or walk to school. Helmets don't keep them safe, good street design does. Unfortunately, Salt Lake City's roads remain super dangerous, especially wider streets with multiple lanes of car traffic and no bicycle lanes at all. Most Utah cities lack a proper network of protected bicycle infrastructure. My willingness and freedom to cycle gets more limited as I get older, sadly. The most effective way to reduce the risk of injury and death to bicycle riders - electric or regular - is to build safe, connected, protected networks of cycle lanes and intersections. Utah's generally big, wide streets give plenty of room to do just that. That is also why I objected so strongly to SB195's assault on SLC's already inadequate safe streets improvements last year. It proved to be a waste of taxpayer money as an unfunded mandate even as the study show that indeed, Salt Lake City's safe multimodal streets upgrades were not "impeded" car traffic. Done right, getting the people willing to take transit or bicycles plus the other proven Traffic Demand Management TDM strategies reduces congestion and traffic. In a growing urban area, it is the only way. SB242's section targeting SLC is much worse despite the results of SB195 that showed SLC is on the right track with rebuilding and redesigning its streets. As the Olympics approach again, SLC needs to keep improving, not fall behind other host cities. This language in SB242 needs to be removed. The Senate vote yesterday was a blow to public safety. May the House members be truly pro-life and stop this. In conclusion, please support HB581 S3 and oppose SB242 unless it is amended as described. Sincerely, Jen Colby, MPA Salt Lake City

subject: Support for Recurring Nuisance Ordinance - City Corner Property
comment: Dear Council Members, I am writing in strong support of the proposed Recurring Nuisance Ordinance scheduled for vote on March 24. I live directly across the street from City Corner convenience store, and for an extended period of time, our neighborhood has experienced ongoing issues connected to this property. These concerns include repeated law enforcement activity, documented undercover investigations related to underage sales of alcohol and vaping products, and consistent traffic of minors entering and exiting the store. This is not an isolated incident. It has become a recurring disruption that affects the safety, stability, and quality of life of surrounding residents. Families live here. Children walk these streets daily. The continued pattern of activity at this location has created an environment that feels unsafe and attracts behavior that does not belong in a residential neighborhood. My understanding is that current enforcement tools often require lengthy criminal proceedings before meaningful action can be taken. In situations like this, that delay allows the nuisance activity to continue for years, despite clear and repeated concerns from neighbors and law enforcement. The Recurring Nuisance Ordinance would provide the City with a more timely and effective tool to address properties that repeatedly generate illegal or disruptive behavior. It creates accountability without requiring years of litigation while the surrounding community continues to bear the impact. This is not about targeting a specific business unfairly. It is about giving the City practical tools to protect neighborhoods when there is an established pattern of documented violations. I respectfully urge you to vote in favor of this ordinance so our community can have a safer and more stable environment. Thank you for your time and service to our city. Sincerely, Liz Rainey

subject: Good news that SB24232 failed in committee, please vote against unless Section 72-20-101 Local Highway Mobility Plans is removed Good news that SB242&2 failed in committee, please vote against unless Section 72-20-101 Local Highway Mobility Plans is removed
comment: Dear Members of the Transportation Committee, I was unable to attend the meeting yesterday but had sent comments in opposition to SB242 S2 and was grateful to learn that it failed to pass. Unfortunately, it returns for another round of review this afternoon. I remain adamantly opposed to SB 242 - Transportation Amendments - as long as it contains Section 72-20-101, Local Highway Mobility Plans, which targets traffic safety infrastructure in Salt Lake City. This undermines public safety, local control, and true freedom of mobility choice. It also violates the House of Representatives' mission statement, as I explain below. Please amend this bill to remove this section. If not, please vote against SB242. I see nothing in this omnibus bill that is critical for this session. Slipping poison pills like this section into an omnibus bill is poor policy making. I have already sent extensive comments about exactly why 72-20-101 is deeply flawed and dangerous. I incorporate them again by reference here. I earned a master's degree in public administration with honors from the University of Utah with a focus on planning and sustainability. I have been an advocate for safe streets, livable and economically vibrant cities, and active mobility for decades so I have expertise in these areas. I also travel a lot and have experienced the great transportation transformations in some of the best cities in the world. If this bill passes with Section 72-20-101, Salt Lake City will have no hope of joining them. I ask you to pause and consider why you are serving as an elected official for the State of Utah and the mission of the House of Representatives. I do believe that you embrace the mission statement and commitment to improving our state. So I don't understand why this bill has been drafted with the section that will not move us forward, but opposite. It is hard to be an expert in everything as a citizen lawmaker. Advocates for this bill section are mistaken. From the House website: https://house.utleg.gov/about-the-house/ The Utah House of Representatives, drawing on the diverse backgrounds and expertise of its members, identifies and leads on critical issues and best ideas in public policy. We honor our pioneer legacy by taking the long view. At the end of our service, we will leave the institution stronger, the State more financially stable, our education systems more nimble, forward-thinking, and responsive to the needs of both students and employers; our healthcare more innovative and affordable; our infrastructure better suited to meet the opportunities of tomorrow; our natural resources—air, water, and incomparable public lands—all better off, protected and preserved to enhance the quality of life for all Utahns. We are proud to represent our constituents and proud to call Utah home. As I read the mission statement, this bill as written violates numerous goals enumerated in it; specifically, the section targeting public safety improvements in Salt Lake City. Here is what I see that is so flawed – I edit the mission statement below as a commentary to reflect what SB242 would do. SB242 lands falls far behind the times on critical issues and best ideas in public policy; it forces dangerous, repeatedly disproven ideas about transportation planning on the capital city and UDOT. Sustainable Safety by design and freedom of mobility due to safe, efficient, multimodal options is best practice. Car dependence by design is what SB242 would create instead. SB242 Dis-honors our pioneer legacy by taking the long-sighted and backwards view. Both Joseph Smith Jr. and Brigham Young were forward-thinking urban planners with clear visions for the Plat of Zion. Salt Lake City was far ahead of its time according to historians as an orderly city complete with public and religious buildings, homes and apartments with gardens and orchards, and major grid streets that were wide enough to accommodate the transition from wagons to cars and also importantly, streetcars and trolleys. The latter system of streetcars was considered visionary for its time. Separated transit corridors on streets were accepted as appropriate street use, in their own dedicated lanes until the trolley lines were torn out and replaced by buses and cars. See Building Zion The Latter-day Saint Legacy of Urban Planning by Craig D. Galli in the BYU Studies Journal for a good article about this. Many cities in Utah including Salt Lake City, Ogden, and West Valley are restoring separated transit lanes on major multiline streets, like TRAX and 200 South and 3500 S. SB242 will leave ....the State more financially stable weakened due to the high cost of car-dependent street design, from the cost of crashes to air pollution to health costs to lower economic activity, and more. It also adds unfunded extra and unnecessary costs to UDOT and Salt Lake City. subject: ACLU: Oppose License Plate Readers
comment: What's at Stake A little-noticed surveillance technology designed to track the movements of every passing driver is fast proliferating on America's streets. Automatic license plate readers—mounted on police cars or on objects like road signs and bridges—use small high-speed cameras to photograph thousands of plates per minute. The information captured by the readers—including the license plate number and the date, time, and location of every scan—is being collected and sometimes pooled into regional sharing systems. As a result, enormous databases of innocent motorists' location information are growing rapidly. This information is often retained for years, or even indefinitely, with few or no restrictions to protect privacy rights. In July 2012, ACLU affiliates in 38 states and Washington, D.C., sent public records act requests to almost 600 local and state police departments, as well as other state and federal agencies, to obtain information on how these agencies use license plate readers. In response, we received thousands of pages of documents detailing the use of the technology around the country. The documents paint a startling picture of a technology deployed with too few rules that is becoming a tool for mass routine location tracking and surveillance. As the technology spreads, the ACLU calls for the adoption of legislation and law enforcement agency policies adhering to strict privacy principles to prevent the government from tracking our movements on a massive scale." https://www.aclu.org/issues/privacy-technology/location-tracking/automatic-license-plate-readers Automatic License Plate Readers | American Civil Liberties Union Thanks, Andrew

subject: Neighborhood Feedback: Concerns Regarding 2027 Long-Term Street Closures
comment: To the City Council and Project Planners, I'm reaching out to share neighborhood concerns I discovered on the proposed six-month street closures planned for 2027. We held a neighborhood meeting on February 18th, and the sentiment from our residents was clear: we are very worried about the effect of the extended time frame for the closures and the impact of the sheer volume of expected visitors, and the resulting impact on cars and parking in our neighborhoods. For those of us in the Capitol Hill community, North and South Temple are our just traffic routes; they are our lifelines to LDS Hospital, Smith's Grocery in the Avenues, and other essential services, including accessing the downtown core and businesses and services on the east side. Closing these major east-west corridors for half a year will be a massive disruption to our daily lives. Based on our community feedback, we are asking the City to address the following: 1. Maintain a Vital East-West Connection: Closing both the North and South Temple streets at the same time is unreasonable. We are asking the City to keep at least one of these major east-west connections open. Without it, you are effectively cutting off our access to the hospital and grocery stores, forcing all neighborhood traffic into a nightmare bottleneck. 2. Parking Protections with "Teeth": A huge portion of our residents rely on street parking only. Between these closures and other downtown events, (i.e. Jazz/Hockey games, concerts like at the Union Event Center, Fairpark events, etc.), and subsequent, simultaneous unrelated and ongoing road/building construction, we are terrified that we won't be able to park anywhere near our own homes for six months. • Temporary Permits: We need the City to issue temporary, enforceable parking permits for residents before the affected blocks. • Real Enforcement: We need a parking plan that has actual "teeth" so that event-goers and commuters aren't taking the few spots our neighbors rely on just to get into their houses. 3. Direct Mitigation Funding: It is equitable that the approximately $2.5 million in fees the City is collecting from the Church be used to support our neighborhoods, which are bearing the burden of these extensive closures in terms of lost access and parking. • Dedicated Enforcement Fund: We are asking for a significant portion of these fees to be set aside specifically for enhanced parking enforcement in Capitol Hill, Avenues, and the West Side during the six-month closure window. We need dedicated officers whose only job is to protect residential permit zones from event-related spillover. • Localized Project Reinvestment: Any remaining funds should be directed towards neighborhood-specific projects. The neighborhood council would be happy to help identify areas within our community where this funding could be redirected. • No "General Fund" Dilution: We strongly oppose these fees being shuffled into the City's general fund for projects across the city. The mitigation should follow the impact. 4. Transit Accountability & Church Communication: Beyond just promoting transit, we need to see the data on how the Church is incentivizing its members to leave their cars at home. • Is the Church coordinating with UTA to provide "event passes" or subsidized transit? What are they doing to actively prevent their members from driving into our residential side-streets to avoid downtown bottlenecks? • Additionally, what specific steps is the Church taking to mitigate these concerns, manage the behavior of their visitors in our area, and how will they address these responsibilities? We understand the ultimate goal is safety for all visitors and the success of the overall event, but it shouldn't come at the expense of our quality of life for half a year. We want to work with all involved, but we need to see a plan that protects our access and our right to park at our own front doors and travel freely through our city. I look forward to hearing how the City plans to address these points. Best, Jake Seastrand

Just so we're clear on what this means for us: Closing these roads funnels everyone who lives west and north either up to the capitol, or south to 200 South. Driving through Marmalade and Capitol Hill is problematic as these are all one-way roads in each direction. 300 North east from 300 West, for example, travels up a steep hill to the capitol, with limited visibility and where drivers often have to pull over to let other cars pass because the road is so narrow. From there drivers have one option: the roundabout in front of the capitol and then south down State Street. That's it—there are no other options because Memory Grove and City Creek Canyon block any travel farther east. The second option pushes people down 300 West or 400 West to 200 South and beyond. 100 South is blocked to the east by the Salt Palace (and drivers can't turn left onto 100 South from West Temple anyway). The bottom line: You're asking thousands of residents to double their commute time. Parents trying to drop their kids off at West High or Bryant Middle School (or, in some cases, both) will be dealing with impossible traffic. Employees trying to get to work downtown will find themselves snarled in traffic in the middle of residential neighborhoods in Capitol Hill, trying to get down State Street. If someone's commute time goes from 10 to 20 minutes, you're asking us to spend an additional 1.5 hours per week (or longer) in our cars. That's 3,000 more minutes spent in a car, not with our kids or friends or doing things we enjoy. Fifty hours—fifty hours spent in our cars over 7 months. It's, I hope you'll agree, asking a lot of residents—too much. If it is determined that these roads must be closed, then the Hive Pass should be made free for residents for the duration of the road closures. Thank you for your consideration and for your service to our city. John Hatch
