subject: 3/10/2026 Meeting: Nuisance Property and Unruly Gathering Enforcement
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Council, As you meet this March 10 to discuss potential enforcement actions on properties that have proven to be a nuisance to their neighbors over the years, I'd like to alert you to the persistent and growing assaults on neighborhood peace and safety experienced by permanent residents throughout the University Gardens neighborhood, just west of the U. of U. Many properties in this area have become de facto satellite fraternities and chronic party houses, frequently hosting large, late-night gatherings associated with unruly behavior including underage drinking, illegal drugs, public urination, extreme noise from outdoor PA systems, yelling, fighting, vandalism and more. Many neighbors have been trying for years to mitigate these problems by communicating with tenants, landlords, the university and the city, but the problems only continue to grow--even despite the recently enacted ordinance that purports to increase accountability for landlords when unruly gatherings occur. Some of us have been threatened, harassed, vandalized and even assaulted when attempting to quiet these gatherings as they happen. I understand that such problems are often considered lower priority for the purpose of police response, but please know that when the same unruly disruptions to our peace and safety happen over and over, year after year, the toll it takes on us is extreme. I, personally, would rather be mugged or assaulted once as opposed to being terrorized out of my peaceful sleep repeatedly for years. I urge you to take whatever actions you can to address this problem while there's still time, before the University Gardens and surrounding neighborhoods are completely and irrecoverably overwhelmed. We need stronger ordinances, stronger enforcement and assured accountability for both landlords and their tenants whenever these issues recur at a given property. Law-abiding permanent residents of this once-wonderful area deserve the promise of peaceful, safe enjoyment of their properties and their neighborhood. Sincerely, Thomas T. Smart

subject: Recurring Nuisance Properties Ordinance
comment: March 9, 2026 Dear Members of the City Council and Mayor Mendenhall: I understand that the City Council will be considering an ordinance relating to nuisance properties, which will include those properties where extremely loud gatherings are held, severely disturbing the peaceful enjoyment of others' homes in the neighborhood. I've lived at my home at 418 Douglas Street since 1994 and have, until recent years, loved the neighborhood. After the past few years, with more and more formerly family homes populated with unrelated people (mostly "students" at the University of Utah), with irresponsible absentee landlords, and with obnoxious, rude, crude tenants and those who attend their parties (who care nothing about the neighbors or the neighborhood), the neighborhood has deteriorated tremendously and the quality of life has been degraded beyond belief. I'm certain property values have been adversely affected as well. I can't imagine anyone with children living through what we've experienced these past few years. Among many other things, during the past few years I have personally witnessed: • An obviously drunk young man urinating in front of dozens of young men and women on an open front yard (I've heard many other accounts of public urination in connection with drunken parties in the neighborhood); • Hordes of drunken young people screaming drunkenly down the middle of the street and on our sidewalks, littering front yards as they go by, on several occasions; • A young man, accompanied by two other young people, drunkenly screaming at the top of his lungs the following antisemitic chant: "The Jews, the Jews, Fuck the Jews, Fuck the Jews, the Jews control everything, Fuck the Jews." When I yelled my own profanities at him and physically pursued him, the three ran into a house and turned out the lights. After I reported the incident, a police officer called and told me she had stopped by the house the next day and no one answered. Case closed. • Numerous drunken parties with many people attending, keeping me and other neighbors up until after mid-night and 1 or 2 a.m. Usually, calls to SLCPD dispatch are unavailing, leaving me with no option (if I want to get any sleep) other than to put my own safety at risk and intervene on my own, with a real risk of violence. I've shut down a few extremely loud parties by going to them by myself and screaming at them. I'd never do that if I thought the police would do their job and put an end to the frequent loud, drunken parties. • Following outrageous parties at homes in our neighborhood, there is often an incredible amount of litter. The tenants at 423 Douglas Street, one of several homes on our block that have held parties keeping me awake until 1 a.m. or later, kept party litter on their front lawn for two full weeks following the last home football game—even after one of them was asked to clean the place up. (Until about four years ago, that home, like so many others, was owned by a woman who had raised her family there. Now, with the neighborhood becoming a party ghetto, the home is inhabited by tenants who host crude, loud, drunk partiers that are an enraging nuisance to our neighborhood.) • On Friday February 27 and early morning Saturday February 28, there were two parties, separated by only a few hours, at the 423 Douglas home. The earlier one broke up when I yelled at them and I was promised by a tenant that there would be no more parties at the house if I wouldn't pursue a nuisance action against the landlord. At 1 a.m., I was awakened by another party at the same address, with a large group of drunk young people yelling so loudly I could hear them from the back of my home. I have an audio recording (which I'd love to share with you) of the extremely loud noise and of me going to where they were (barefooted and wearing what I'd worn to bed) and yelling at them. That's what it took for them to break up the party, with profuse, drunken apologies. I was recently trading stories with a neighbor about us walking our dogs, who far too often approach puddles of human vomit left by drunken young partiers in our neighborhood. Scooters blocking the sidewalks, puddles of vomit, broken bottles and other party litter now define in large part the experience of what it is to walk in my neighborhood. Truly, that's what it is to live in this degraded neighborhood these days, thanks to the lack of enforcement of laws by the police and by the person employed by the City who is supposed to process warning letters and fines for landlords of properties where unruly parties are held. Dozens of neighbors, including me, are frequently doing the jobs that the SLCPD and the City should be doing to patrol, report, and try to put an end to obscenely loud and obnoxious parties attended by young people who clearly don't care about their impacts on neighbors and our neighborhoods. We share messages frequently about loud drunken gatherings and about the usual lack of enforcement by police officers. (There have been some admirable exceptions, but far too few and infrequent.) One is left totally baffled as to why the police do not, once and for all, nip this problem in the bud by aggressively patrolling and enforcing the laws on nights when partying is foreseeable and provide the evidence and other information necessary for warnings to landlords and fines. It has been apparent that many police officers are not properly trained regarding the several tools available to enforce against the parties that are so significantly undermining our quality of life. Also, why are obviously drunken, obnoxious young people not arrested for underage drinking, possession by a minor, public intoxication, disturbing the peace, vandalism, littering, and drunk driving when it happens so frequently and is clearly illegal? Also, why in the world did the City eliminate progressive fines against the tenants of homes where loud parties are being held? When I was mayor, we assessed progressively larger fines against tenants AND landlords. We aggressively enforced – and it worked. Every City Council member and the Mayor, as well as the Chief of Police, should review the neighbors' reports, photos, videos, and audio recordings on the WhatsApp account on which we share our communications. They tell a harrowing story of a neighborhood and quality of life being destroyed—and the City's utter failure to do its job in enforcing the law and effectively deterring the frequent out-of-control noisy drunken parties. With the permission of others communicating on that account, I'd be pleased to provide the reports, photos, videos, and audio recordings to members of the news media. I urge that every possible tool be provided by the City to put this nightmare to an end. (And please require only two, and not three, outrageous noisy parties for a nuisance action to be commenced.) And please make certain that those who are responsible for returning and maintaining peace in our neighborhoods, including the police and the person responsible for warning/fining landlords, do their job aggressively and effectively. Thank you for finally focusing on this serious problem and helping to devise remedies that can restore our neighborhoods. Sincerely, Ross C. "Rocky" Anderson

subject: Nuisance properties.
comment: I have lived in the university Historic District for 35 years. Never have we had as many problems with noise and unruly households as we do now- many of them affiliated with fraternities and sororities. This issue has very much negatively impacted the quality of life here and our property values. It used to be our neighborhood was considered a desirable place to live (Douglas Street in particular). Now we are experiencing what I would call reverse gentrification. I believe part of the problem is that the University Of Utah cracked down on the fraternities near campus because of this sort of behavior and they have offloaded these problems to satellite houses in our neighborhood. This is unacceptable. How this issue typically manifest itself is that a party will start early in mid-afternoon at one address with lots of underage drinking, noise (loud penetrating bass that goes through all the surrounding houses and you cannot get away from for hours), garbage, and beer pong tables set up in the front yard. If the cops come, they don't cite them... They simply tell them to turn it down. (This may be partly a misunderstanding on the part of the police, who are perhaps unaware of the Unruly Property ordinance, and look at the issue more as a "noise issue". It is not. It is an unruly household and needs to be cited under the existing ordinance.) Since this may be during the afternoon (or before 10:00 PM), they don't issue a citation, they just say please turn it down, you're bothering your neighbors. (I don't know why the hell they are not ticketing for all the under-age drinking(?)), If the police do shut that address down, the problem metastasizes to another satellite frat house and starts up there... With a response time of sometimes several hours for the police, this quickly becomes a losing whack-a-mole game that goes later and later into the evening and results in hordes of very drunk students yelling and screaming obscenities as they walk up and down our streets after midnight. (let me know if you want me to demonstrate what that is like in front of your own homes). As council members, I want you to take a moment to pause and think about what it would be like to plan on being woken several times during the week by drunk kids yelling and screaming obscenities as they walk in front of your house at two in the morning, as the parties break up... many of them also getting into cars and driving drunk through your neighborhood. To fix this, we need the police to start doing their jobs under the existing Unruly house ordinance and citing the the landlords--not simply telling these students to turn it down and then going away for them to then turn it back up or move to another address to start up again. Out of all the numerous calls that have been made to the police over this issue, there have been only six actual citations resulting in fines to the landlord. That is completely unacceptable. Because of this, there is a group of us that are considering legal action if this problem does not immediately change significantly for the better. There are hundreds of homes in this area negatively affected by this issue and their combined value is easily north of $100 million dollars. This situation we feel is related to: 1. A failure of enforcement on the part of the City and 2. Negligence on the part of the University Of Utah in the handling of the fraternal organizations. It may compel us to file lawsuits against both the City and the University of Utah seeking damages for our lost property values and the negative impacts on our lives. This could result in potentially tens of millions of dollars in damages sought. Please make this ordinance better and most importantly, please start enforcing it by providing adequate education to the police officers involved so that they quickly move to citations as appropriate, as well as citations under existing laws for other illegal activities occurring on the sites. Thank you, Joe Arnold

subject: Nuisance Ordinance March 10th for Discussion
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Council Members, I am writing as a concerned resident about the ongoing unruly parties and nuisance activity in our neighborhood. After living here for 33 years, I can say without hesitation that the behavior has become more intense, more disrespectful, and at times genuinely dangerous. Over the years I have witnessed underage drinking, students running into traffic, drunken driving accidents, and "honk and we drink" signs encouraging reckless behavior on our streets. I have seen three separate cars crashes into the maple trees and bushes in front of our home, with intoxicated students stumbling away and abandoning their vehicles on our lawn to avoid a DUI. One of those trees—the one my children built a treehouse in—was eventually removed by the city because the repeated damage from these accidents killed it. A few years ago, my grandfather, a proud University of Utah alumnus, walked these blocks with me. As we stepped over beer cans and tried to ignore the shouting, profanity, and racial slurs coming from gatherings along University Street across from The Law School, he said bluntly, "This neighborhood sure has gone downhill." It was painful to hear, because this is the neighborhood where my husband and I chose to live after graduating from the University of Utah, and where we have raised our family. It is the neighborhood we have loved. But it is becoming harder to love. Neighbors I care deeply about have been called slurs, threatened, and had their homes egged or otherwise damaged by intoxicated partygoers. Our own home was egged after we politely asked a nearby party to lower the noise. That gathering later escalated into drugs, fighting, blaring music, and students stumbling to their cars at 2:00 AM to drive away intoxicated. Our sprinkling system has been pulled out of the ground by intoxicated students. And our yard has become a stop and puke space for drunken students. On another night, while trying to sleep, I overheard a student get run over in the driveway next door by another drunk student. The victim laughed it off, saying they were too drunk to feel anything. But when that same car hit our iron fence, I was certainly awake. This behavior persists in part because the system meant to address it is not working for residents. When police have responded—often after multiple calls reporting underage drinking, fighting, drugs, public urination, and large unruly parties—they have sometimes apologized to the party hosts while asking if a fight had occurred. I personally overheard this. Meanwhile, the party of forty or more people continued at 1:30 in the morning. It went on for another hour. I did not sleep that night. For context, we also live just six doors down from the house where a stabbing years ago took the life of a University of Utah football player. These situations are not hypothetical concerns—they are real safety risks. The sidewalk can also be deeply disrespectful. I have come home to find a college-aged man urinating directly next to my car, in front of my passenger window. When my husband asked him to stop, the student replied that he "couldn't stop once he started." The yard beside our driveway has effectively become a public restroom for partygoers when a single bathroom cannot accommodate the dozens—sometimes close to a hundred—people drinking at these gatherings. For years, residents have tried to resolve these problems through conversations with tenants, landlords, and city departments. Despite those efforts, the situation has only escalated and continues to erode the safety, livability, and basic dignity of our neighborhood. I have had great neighbors and friends who have left the neighborhood to reclaim their sanity and sleep. Our closest neighbor had her halloween decorations stolen and destroyed, only to show up decorating the opposite party neighbors home. The seriousness of allowing this to continue has left my husband and I, with one single family home left on our street. All of our best neighbors and friends have left our block due to the ongoing and UNRULY behaviors, only perpetuating the problem when absent landlords rent to these students causing such nuisances. While I appreciate the City's efforts to address nuisance activity through ordinance, stronger and more consistent enforcement is clearly needed. Without meaningful consequences, the behavior simply continues. I urge the City Council to strengthen enforcement of nuisance violations, hold property owners accountable for repeated problems at their properties, implement clear penalties for repeat offenders, and ensure that police and code enforcement have the resources needed to respond effectively. Residents have done everything we can on our own. We now need the City's help to restore safety, accountability, and peace in our neighborhood. Sincerely, Stacie Lawrence Kindergarten Teacher, Salt Lake City School District Mom and Wife

subject: Neighborhood Safety and Unruly Gathering Enforcement
comment: City Council Members, I am writing to express my support for stronger enforcement of Salt Lake City's nuisance activity ordinance, particularly regarding unruly gatherings and repeated disruptive behavior. As a homeowner in the East Central neighborhood for over 20 years, I have noted an increase in large parties which spill into the street, resulting in excessive late night noise, vandalism, and unsafe behavior over the past several years. Neighbors have made every effort to establish relationships with the tenants and landlords of these residences rather than engage law enforcement, yet problem houses are increasingly emboldened, recognizing that Salt Lake City enforcement and accountability has no teeth. Not only do these unruly gatherings disrupt the peace, but they pose real safety concerns. Requiring law enforcement to witness the behavior on more than one occasion before any penalty is levied is clearly problematic. Law enforcement is overtaxed and may have more pressing concerns; furthermore, their presence may escalate a situation rather than have the desired effect of restoring the peace. Any ordinance should consider allowing for video evidence or corroborating accounts from 3 or more neighbors as supporting evidence rather than further burdening law enforcement. Please ensure that this ordinance includes strong enforcement tools, accountability for landlords with repeat nuisance properties, and increased penalties for repeat offenders. All residents deserve safe, peaceful neighborhoods- we need the city's help to restore safety and accountability in our neighborhood. Sincerely, Tammy Smith- East Central Neighborhood

comment: The neighbors bear the burden of these potential street closures. Increased times for emergency vehicles to navigate to our neighborhood, slower exit from the neighborhood which is particularly troubling in an emergency, general frustration in trying to get anywhere, particularly during rush hour, from the Capitol Hill neighborhood. This is all for another extended period of time. Definitely not in our community's best interest. The church has many avenues to reduce the number of people coming to visit at once. Timed entry, must have a ticket or reservation for a time slot. Reducing the amount of people daily, extending daily visiting hours. They can take a year to celebrate the renovations to accommodate everyone. The church is well versed in managing large crowds as they do that 2 times a year already. Hate to say it, but it feels like the beginning of a push to have a permanent 'Vatican' like space for the church. I'm sure the city could use the $$$ offered to off set costs, but in the end, our neighborhood loses. Rhonda Devereaux

subject: Proposed N. Temple Closures
comment: Dear Council members, Having served two terms on the Transportation Advisory Board, I feel moved to respectfully point out to the Council that closure of North Temple will exacerbate existing bottlenecks (explanation follows) effectively trapping residents in the high density zones between A Street and Canyon Road, and centered on 3rd Avenue, in their neighborhoods during periods of closure. Likewise impeded will be residents of Canyon Road, and City Creek users. Explanation of current conditions: 1. 3rd Avenue is one way to the West and these residents have no other exit. 2. 3rd Avenue drains all traffic to Canyon Road, which drains to 2nd Avenue. Westbound 2nd Avenues becomes N. Temple at State Street. 3. the lack of a protected left turn from Westbound 2nd Avenue to State Street saturates the holding lanes of 2nd Avenue at State at traffic peaks. 4. the installation of an inadequately sized traffic circle at State Street and 300 North, which fails when traffic is present at all entries, routinely backs up Northbound State as far as 2nd and State. 5. an unprotected left turn from Canyon Road onto Eastbound 2nd Avenue is the only other exit from Canyon Road. During closure intervals this will likely be exacerbated to the point it will prevent exit for these residents without police intervention and long delays. Residents will, and should, find this situation unacceptable. The LDS Church leadership has the right to make a big spectacle out of the Temple reopening, but surely, with their vast resources, they can find a way to do so without such extensive negative impacts to City residents. If the closure becomes a reality, I hope the City can effectively provide relief to these residents, as well as others. Yours Sincerely, Jim Jenkin

subject: Unruly Gatherings, City Council meeting tonight
comment: Subject: Support for Stronger Enforcement of Nuisance Activity Ordinance Dear Salt Lake City Council Members, I am writing as a resident of the neighborhood affected by ongoing unruly gatherings and nuisance activity. For years, residents have attempted to resolve these issues through communication with property owners, tenants, and city departments, yet the problem continues to escalate. Late-night parties, excessive noise, public intoxication, vandalism, and disruptive conduct have become increasingly common and are severely impacting the safety, livability, and stability of our neighborhood. As a 30+ year resident of the University district, I can attest to the worsening behavior and frequency of such. I have had 3 windows broken, 2 in the last year. I have been awoken at 2 am with noise from parties and marauding hordes of men. While I appreciate the city addressing nuisance activity through this ordinance, enforcement must be strong, consistent, and meaningful. Without real consequences, the behavior will continue. Residents have done everything we can to mitigate these problems ourselves. We now need the City's help to restore safety and accountability in our neighborhood. Sincerely, Judith Warner, University neighborhood

comment: To whom it may concern, This message represents Wyatt Millar, Rishi Madhireddy, Carson Pollock, and James Williams. We are residents of REDACTED in Salt Lake City. It has been brought to our attention that the Salt Lake City Council is reconsidering noise ordinances regarding alleged late-night parties and excessive noise. As residents, we possess the right to gather and socialize on private property outside of established quiet hours. Given that the undergraduate experience is formative period of our lives, we deserve the opportunity to form a community with other students through gatherings and barbecues. In our personal experience, we have created fantastic memories and developed incredible friendships by inviting friends and neighbors into our home. The gatherings we host possess zero malicious intent, but create safe and welcoming environments. Our home has garnered a positive reputation in the past couple months, and we would like to continue to create a safe space. Lastly, it is pertinent to consider the timing of this meeting. Sincerely, Wyatt Millar, Rishi Madhireddy, Carson Pollock, and James Williams

subject: Public Comment for City Council Meeting 3/10
comment: Greetings, I am close acquaintances with some current residents in this HOA community as well as a caregiver for a family in the same community. I am aware that this area draws in a great community of newly weds, college students, and other young folks who are starting out their independent lives. I am also aware that the current "quiet hours" for this area is 10pm. Myself and my close friends who live here completely abide by these rules and the laws. We safely and legally have small gatherings with our close friends, enjoying the community together by having barbecues or playing board games, etc. We do not partake in loud outdoor music, illegal activities, or disruptive behavior. We simply are exercising our right to community. It would be extremely isolating and dampening to this community that so many love to ban the innocent, friendly community building that goes on in this area. If we are respecting the rules and laws that tell us to have everything done and over by 10pm, there should not be punishment. This is an extremely rash decision that would upset and cause mental health issues in the area. Most young, newcomers are searching for that sense of belonging and community, and taking that away and banning innocent fun would be unfair and cruel. I understand not all people follow the current rules, and I believe that they should be the ones facing the punishments as it is their doing. Becoming stricter on the preexisting rules seems like a fair compromise for all in this community. I sincerely hope you take a second to consider these words and the words from the rest of the community. Thank you

subject: Neighborhood Concerns Regarding Student Tenants
comment: To whom it my concern, My name is Aaron Maxfield. I grew up on the REDACTED in Salt Lake City, and I have owned rental properties in the area for over 10 years. During that time, I have always made it a priority to place responsible, respectful tenants in my properties. Some of the best tenants I have had the privilege of renting to have been students. Over the past six months, I have received a number of calls and text messages reporting that my tenants were hosting loud and disruptive parties. Each time I received one of these complaints, I responded immediately to investigate the situation. In nearly every case, I found that there was little to no disturbance. In several instances, the complaints were made as early as 4 or 5 in the afternoon. I want to be clear that I am strongly opposed to any behavior that interferes with a neighbor's right to peacefully enjoy their property. In fact, I have evicted tenants in the past for conduct that crossed that line. However, what I have observed in recent months does not appear to be an issue of loud or disrespectful parties. Instead, it seems that students themselves are being unfairly targeted. Students have the same right as any other resident to gather in their backyard and spend time with friends, provided they are doing so respectfully and within the law. Living just one or two blocks from one of the most outstanding universities in Utah naturally comes with some challenges, but overall it has been a positive and vibrant part of our neighborhood. Of course, loud and disruptive parties late at night should be addressed. However, targeting or criticizing students who are simply gathering and following the rules is neither fair nor productive. In my experience, the Salt Lake City police have done an excellent job responding to complaints—issuing citations where appropriate and also recognizing when no laws or ordinances are being violated. I will continue to do everything I can to ensure my properties are well-managed and that our neighborhood continues to grow and improve. Thank you for your time. Best regards, Aaron Maxfield

subject: Formal Objection to Proposed Quiet Hour Changes
comment: To the Salt Lake City Council, I am writing as a supportive friend and long-term guest of the residents at REDACTED. It has come to our attention that the HOA is considering shortening the standard window for social activity by moving quiet hours earlier than the established norms of our city and state. On behalf of Wyatt, Rishi, Carson, and James, I am urging the board to maintain a schedule that aligns with the standard 10:00 PM to 7:00 AM window used by Salt Lake City and Salt Lake County. Imposing a more restrictive "curfew" is not only professionally unnecessary but creates an impractical environment for residents balancing academic and social lives. Our argument for maintaining the 10:00 PM standard is based on three pillars: 1. Consistency with Local Law and Civic Standards Salt Lake City (and Salt Lake County) has established 10:00 PM as the professional threshold for residential quiet hours. This standard exists because it represents a fair balance between the right to rest and the right to social liberty. By deviating from this, the HOA risks creating a "policing" environment that is more restrictive than the law itself, which often leads to unnecessary friction and a decrease in resident satisfaction. 2. Legal Precedent and "Reasonable Use" Under the Utah Community Association Act (57-8a-218), HOA rules generally should not interfere with activities within a dwelling that comply with local ordinances unless those activities constitute a genuine "nuisance." The current residents at REDACTED have maintained a safe, welcoming, and respectful environment. Shortening quiet hours effectively "redlines" their ability to engage in standard social behaviors—like hosting a dinner or a small weekend gathering—that are perfectly legal and common throughout the rest of the city. 3. Preserving the "Social Fabric" of the Neighborhood The undergraduate years are a vital time for building community. These residents have worked hard to build a positive reputation and a safe space for their peers. Moving quiet hours to an earlier time (such as 8:00 PM or 9:00 PM) creates a "dormitory" atmosphere that is inconsistent with the reality of living in a vibrant, urban neighborhood near a major university. It penalizes responsible residents for the sake of an arbitrary standard that does not reflect the lifestyle of the community's majority. A neighborhood thrives when rules are predictable and fair. We believe that the current 10:00 PM standard is the most professional and equitable solution for all parties involved. We hope the board will choose to align with Salt Lake City's established ordinances rather than imposing further restrictions. Sincerely, Kal Shays

Videos of the party and the noise? Something needs to be done as it is affecting the quality of life for those in the neighborhood. Thank you for your time, Sallie Shatz

subject: Residents Need Real Solutions to Ongoing Nuisance Issues
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Council, For many years, residents in our neighborhood have been dealing with ongoing nuisance activity, including large late-night parties, excessive noise, public intoxication, and property damage. Neighbors have repeatedly attempted to resolve these issues by speaking with tenants, contacting landlords, and reporting incidents to the city. Unfortunately, despite these efforts, the situation has continued to worsen. The current system often allows repeat offenders to continue disruptive behavior without meaningful consequences. We support the city's efforts to address nuisance activity, but the ordinance must include strong enforcement and accountability, including holding property owners responsible for repeated nuisance activity, stronger penalties for repeat incidents, increased enforcement presence in problem areas, and clear pathways for residents to report and track violations. Residents should not have to endure ongoing disruption and safety concerns in their own neighborhood.

subject: Request for Stronger Enforcement and Accountability for Nuisance Properties
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Council Members, My name is Nathan Starley. My husband and I first moved into the Douglas neighborhood as renters in the fall of 2006, and we purchased our home here in October of 2008. We live one block southwest of the U. I am also a graduate of the University of Utah and rented in this area myself during college. For many years we loved living in this neighborhood because it felt safe and connected to the university community. Unfortunately, over the past several years the situation has changed dramatically. An increasing number of nearby homes have transitioned into high-turnover rental properties that regularly host extremely large gatherings. These are not occasional celebrations. These are frequent disruptive parties that spill into surrounding streets and yards and occur at all times of day — sometimes beginning in the morning or early afternoon and continuing late into the night. The impact on the neighborhood is significant. The noise is not only heard outside; residents often hear crowds and music inside their homes even with the windows closed. In some cases speakers placed on the ground send vibrations through the ground and into surrounding houses. At the same time, intoxicated crowds move through residential streets yelling, leaving trash, urinating in yards, and sometimes vandalizing nearby homes. This affects everyone — homeowners, renters, and even other students who simply want a quiet place to live and study. My husband and I have spent years trying to address this issue through every available channel. We have contacted property owners, spoken directly with tenants, worked with the university, called law enforcement, and documented repeated disturbances. We have spent countless hours trying to resolve these issues appropriately. Despite those efforts, many residents feel that nothing changes. In fact, many feel the situation has worsened over time, and some long-time residents and renters have chosen to move away because of the ongoing disturbances. A recent incident on February 28 illustrates how serious the situation has become. During a large gathering at a nearby rental property, intoxicated individuals leaving the party moved through the neighborhood late at night. When my husband and I simply asked people to keep the noise down out of consideration for nearby families and elderly residents, eggs were thrown at our home and we were subjected to homophobic slurs. Police responded and documented the incident. No one should feel unsafe in their own home for asking for basic respect. This issue is not about preventing students from enjoying their college experience. It is about ensuring that a small number of repeat nuisance properties do not negatively disrupt an entire neighborhood. I respectfully urge the City to consider stronger nuisance property enforcement measures, including: • Fines tied directly to the property for repeat disturbances • Greater accountability for landlords whose properties repeatedly host nuisance activity • Stronger enforcement within the Good Landlord Program, including loss of incentives for repeat violations • Ensuring rental licensing and compliance are actively enforced • Enforcement of the $1,000 fine (I heard only 5 have been issued out all the many, many disturbances and reported disturbances since this was enacted) These types of tools can help ensure that a small number of problem properties do not continue to negatively impact an entire neighborhood. Everyone deserves the quiet enjoyment of their home and to feel safe where they live. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Nathan Starley Douglas Neighborhood Resident

subject: City council meeting March 10, 2026 - Urgent Request for Stronger Enforcement on Ongoing Nuisance Party Houses in Our Neighborhood
comment: I am writing as a long-time resident who is deeply concerned about the ongoing issues our neighborhood is facing with repeated nuisance party houses and the lack of effective enforcement to address them. My partner and I have lived in our home for nearly 19 years. We chose this neighborhood because of its strong sense of community and because it has historically been a place where neighbors look out for one another. Over the past several years, however, the situation with large student party houses has steadily worsened and has reached a point where many residents feel unsafe and unheard. For more than four and a half years, our neighborhood has been dealing with repeated large and disruptive gatherings at rental properties. One property in particular, 1233 E 600 S, has been a significant source of disturbance since approximately October 2024. These gatherings routinely involve large crowds late into the night, loud music, shouting, and people spilling out into surrounding yards and streets. Residents frequently have to call the police simply to restore basic peace in the neighborhood. Unfortunately, the issue does not end when police disperse the parties. In many cases, this is when a secondary and often more damaging problem begins. Groups of partygoers leave the property and walk through the neighborhood yelling, screaming, vandalizing property, and disturbing residents as they disperse. Neighbors have witnessed underage drinking, public intoxication, and individuals leaving these gatherings and driving while impaired, which raises very serious public safety concerns. This past weekend the situation escalated in a way that no resident should have to experience. During a gathering in the area, individuals vandalized our home by throwing eggs at our house, causing property damage that we are now having assessed. While doing so, they repeatedly yelled homophobic slurs including "fags" and "faggots." The harassment was aggressive and deeply unsettling. Police responded and documented the incident under case number 26-47172, and we have preserved video footage and documentation. After nearly two decades in this neighborhood, it is heartbreaking to feel that our home — the place where we have invested years of our lives — has become a place where we must install cameras and security measures simply to feel safe. I want to emphasize that this is not about being anti-student or anti-university. Many students are wonderful neighbors. The issue is a systemic pattern of nuisance properties where tenants host repeated large gatherings with little accountability, and the surrounding neighborhood bears the consequences. What we are asking for is straightforward: • Stronger and more consistent enforcement of nuisance and disorderly conduct laws • Greater accountability for property owners who allow repeated nuisance activity • Better coordination to address the secondary issue of large groups dispersing through neighborhoods causing damage and disturbances • Clear consequences that deter repeat behavior Residents should not have to spend years documenting disturbances, installing security systems, and contacting city officials just to protect their homes. We love this neighborhood and want it to remain a place where families, long-term residents, and students can coexist respectfully. But without stronger enforcement and accountability, the current trajectory is not sustainable. We will be attending the upcoming council meeting and hope the City will take meaningful action to address these ongoing issues. Thank you for your time and for your commitment to our community. Best Regards,

subject: Temple Square Street Closures
comment: Esteemed Council, As the petition to close North Temple during the Salt Lake Temple Open House is considered, it may be helpful to also account for the daily transportation needs of the many students, parents, faculty, and staff who travel to West High School from the Avenues, Federal Heights, and other neighborhoods east of downtown. North Temple serves as one of the most direct east–west routes to the school. If both North Temple and South Temple are closed, families and buses will likely be pushed several blocks farther south, creating longer and more complex commutes—particularly challenging for student drivers who are still gaining experience. Those detours may also place school traffic into already busy areas near the Salt Palace and Delta Center. School bus routes that normally use North Temple would also be affected. Delays could make it difficult for students to arrive on time, and some may miss the opportunity to eat breakfast at school—whether through the free breakfast program or by purchasing a meal. Adjusting bus schedules to compensate may be difficult, given existing driver shortages and the complexity of coordinating routes that serve multiple stops before reaching West High. Reliable access to the school is important not only in the morning and afternoon but also in the evenings, when many families return for performances, games, and meetings. Parents sometimes need to reach the school quickly during the day as well. Detouring traffic as far south as 400 South in order to cross downtown and then return north could add several miles of stop-and-go driving to each trip and significantly increase travel times for families commuting between the Avenues and West High. With these factors in mind, it may be worth exploring whether there are alternatives that could accommodate visitors to Temple Square while still preserving practical access to the school. Possibilities might include a temporary pedestrian bridge across North Temple or temporarily allowing two-way traffic through City Creek Canyon during school days. The surrounding community has adapted to years of construction and lane reductions in this area, often with the understanding that full closures would be limited to weekends, evenings, or non-school days. Ensuring that students and families can continue to reach their neighborhood public school reliably each day would be deeply appreciated as part of this decision-making process. Thank you, Havilah Zeller Constituent District 3

subject: Community Perspective on Proposed Restrictions Near the University
comment: Hello, my name is Cali Dillon, and I am a resident living near the university. I am writing regarding the recent concerns about parties and gatherings in the neighborhood. I understand that there have been some instances where parties have gotten out of hand, and I agree that those situations should absolutely be addressed. I want this neighborhood to be a safe place to live for everyone, and I do not support unsafe or disruptive gatherings. At the same time, I do not believe it is fair for the entire community to face strict restrictions because of the actions of a small number of people. Many students who live in this area are respectful neighbors who do not participate in large or disruptive parties. In fact, some of us have built positive relationships with the people who live around us and work to maintain friendly and respectful connections within the neighborhood. We care about the community we live in and want to continue being good neighbors. It would be unfortunate if responsible residents were prevented from simply having friends over, hosting small gatherings, or spending time with others in lawful and respectful ways because of a few isolated incidents. I believe the better approach would be to address and enforce rules specifically when problematic behavior occurs, rather than placing broad restrictions on everyone. This neighborhood exists alongside a university, and naturally that means students will be part of the community. College towns across the country balance the presence of students while still maintaining safe and respectful neighborhoods. With fair enforcement and clear expectations, it is possible to address unsafe behavior while still allowing responsible residents to live normally. I hope the council will consider solutions that focus on the specific problems without placing unnecessary limitations on the many residents who are doing their best to contribute positively to the community. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Cali Dillon

subject: Public comment on street closures
comment: Wasn't able to finish.... Here's my complete comment... Good evening and thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed street closures My name is Rob Kertesz. I live right across the street from Temple Square and I serve on the board of the Downtown Community Council. I'd like to share our council's thoughts on the proposed street closures associated with the Salt Lake Temple open house. First, we want to thank The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints for its clear effort to be a good neighbor as it prepares for this event. We especially appreciate the staggered workforce schedules, the transit passes offered to employees, the attention to pedestrian safety, and the plans for off-site parking and shuttle service. These steps show a real effort to reduce pressure on downtown streets and parking. At the same time, closing several city streets for an extended period raises important questions about balancing major events with everyday downtown life. Downtown Salt Lake City is not just an event space—it is a neighborhood where people live, work, run businesses, receive deliveries, and depend on reliable street access. The North Temple closure alone affects several UTA bus routes and one of the key connections between downtown and the west side. For these reasons, we echo the concerns already expressed by city council members and encourage the city and the church to continue working closely with residents and businesses to ensure clear timelines, strong communication, and dependable access during the open house period. We also see the closure as an opportunity. Temporary closures could help the city evaluate whether more pedestrian- and bicycle-friendly streets might work downtown in the future. Finally, one constructive step would be offering free transit access on during the open house—partnering with the city to offer free public transit for everyone, not just church employees and their guests. This event will bring the world to Salt Lake City, and it is also an opportunity to show how a city and a major institution work together to care for the people who live and work here every day. Rob Kertesz

subject: My comments about proposed SLC Temple celebration street closures - please postpone vote until issues can be addressed
comment: Dear Members of the City Council and Mayor's Office, Below are the prepared personal comments that I read at the March 10 council meeting hearing regarding the "Temporary Street Closures for 2027 Temple Reopening Celebration." I believe the proposal should be substantially modified prior to adoption of any ordinance to truly meet the goals of safety, access, and traffic mitigation. Given the celebration is more than a year away, there is plenty of time to do so. To put it mildly, this proposed closure is simply not comparable to any previous event closures since I have lived in Salt Lake City - including the 2002 Olympics. A seven-eight month complete, fenced-off public closure for the 2 major streets in question is unparalleled. After attending the hearing and doing more research, I am even more concerned that this proposal is not adequate as drafted. Many specific questions have been raised and more details should be clarified. Existing car traffic counts have not been provided nor estimates of additional traffic due to the celebration even with some TDM (travel demand management). Cycling counts and access is also ignored. Visitor estimates seem like guesses. Given that this will be a ticketed event with specific opening times and visitor capacity controlled, planners should be able to better predict and manage daily attendance. If the temple is closed to visitors on Sundays, why are closures needed those days? Ditto during the closed hours - from 9 pm to 9 am if the general Temple Square summer hours are representative. Instead, the exisitng model of temporary closures during the Corporation of the President of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' General Conferences is much more appropriate and far less disruptive. From their website: https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/events/temple-square-guidelines?lang=eng : Temporary Road Closures to Ensure Safety During major events in the Conference Center, North Temple between Main Street and West Temple will be restricted to pedestrian access. Restrictions will start two hours before the event. (see diagram of the movable barriers, not fencing, on that webpage). I will send additional comments in a separate message but wanted to get my initial public comments into the written record. Sincerely, Jen Colby, MPA East Central District 4 Salt Lake City resident I support open streets events and pedestrianized urban zones. But looking closer at this proposal I have serious concerns and ask that the ordinance be revised. We are still a year out so please do not rush to vote on this until these issues are resolved. I am glad to see that event organizers recognize that it is the cars that are the problem and safety threat, not the people outside of cars. If only they would argue for safer streets by design more broadly. Anyway, my concerns here include the exclusivity clause, the proposed fencing, the scope of the closures, and potential discrimination. I object to the apparent closure of the streets to bicyclists, especially in the critical West Temple lanes. The 10-acre blocks make walking and bicycling detours burdensome especially given the lack of a complete, safe, protected bike lane network downtown. I ask that the car traffic be blocked with appropriate barricades, but no fencing be allowed. I do not think Salt Lake City should sell out the people's rights of general public access to our streets. The city should simply temporarily restrict the ability of car drivers to use them. I also suggest considering only the closure of eastbound North Temple in both blocks and only the northbound car lane of West Temple. Several UTA buses use North Temple and celebration visitors and residents alike should be able to use them. I am particularly worried about potential discriminatory actions against certain groups of people, especially if the exclusionary zones are fenced and access points are controlled by the Church. President Oaks has led the legal charge to maintain a religious privilege to discriminate. This is currently aimed mostly at people who identify as LGBTQIA+. All people should be able to use our public streets and sidewalks freely and without fear of bias or discrimination. Please do not sell out these rights, even temporarily. Therefore, I ask that you: • Modify the language of the ordinance to remove the word "exclusive." • Also please add a section that specifies full non-discrimination during the closure for all people. Restricted access should only be for private cars. • Please also forbid fencing closures. With those changes and other community suggestions, this could be a wonderful open streets season that truly celebrates the restored Salt Lake Temple and welcomes the world. As is, unfortunately it may risk driving more division and community conflict. In times such as these, peacemaking is sorely needed. Thank you.

subject: Opposition to street closures for LDS temple open house
comment: Dear Olivia Erickson, I live in Chris Wharton's district and am, in fact, his neighbor. I have owned a home at REDACTED in Salt Lake since 1984. I am writing to urge Chris and all other city council members to vote against the LDS church's request to close streets and traffic lanes around the temple for six months in 2027. I believe the request is extremely unreasonable and not in the best interest of the residents of Salt Lake City. I would feel differently if their request were for a two or three week period of time, similar to changes that were instituted during the 2002 Olympics; such a short time period is temporary enough that it would be a reasonable request. However, a six month period of road closures/lane reductions is not even close to reasonable. This is especially true because of other closures and lane reductions already underway in the same area, or planned for the same time period - construction of the Salt Palace, the West High School construction, and construction in the area of the Delta Center. In addition, 200 West is closed off fairly regularly when the Salt Palace has events to create a parking area for large trucks west of the Salt Palace. Of course, Main Street has been permanently closed between North and South Temple for many years after Salt Lake City allowed the LDS church to purchase it to create parking for itself. All of this means that residents like me and others who live in my neighborhood will struggle to find a way to get into, or out of, our homes because of the lack of accessible roads. In addition, having daily crowds in/near our neighborhood equivalent to the crowds we already endure for the LDS church's general conferences will be, frankly, awful. During those conferences, cars usually fill up the parking places in front of my home and the homes of my neighbors, leaving no place for us to park. For two days twice a year, it's annoying and inconvenient, but we can deal with it. However, having that occur every day for 6 months would be an unreasonable burden. If the city council does vote to allow the church to close roads/reduce lanes as they have requested, I suggest some methods to mitigate the effects and inconvenience to residents affected by the measures, such as: 1. Greatly shorten the time period where it will be allowed. Two weeks or even one month is much more reasonable than the current six month request. 2. Require the church to pay the construction companies who are doing work in the neighborhood during this time period to cease construction while the open house sessions are occurring so additional road closures/lane reductions are not happening then. 3. Create Resident Only parking areas in the affected neighborhoods, giving us residents parking permits to park on the streets by our homes, and prohibiting visitors to the temple from parking in our neighborhoods.Although some Resident Only parking is already in place near my home, it does not exist for 200 West and, I believe, streets west of 200 West. Also, I suggest requiring the church to pay for increased numbers of persons to be hired as SLC parking enforcement employees to ticket parking violators. The parking violation fees should be shared with the residents who are impacted by the parking violations. 4. Require the church to pay a monthly stipend to residents who are impacted by either/both the street closures and visitors parking in front of our homes. I think it's likely that residents would be considerably more forgiving of the many problems created by the open house sessions if we received payments from the church of, for instance, $500.00 per month. The LDS church is a wealthy institution and can certainly afford to provide such stipends. 5. Disallow the closure of 200 West behind the Salt Palace for truck parking during the time period of the open house sessions, thus assuring that the street will be open to traffic. For all of these reasons, I urge Chris and other city council members to vote against the church's request for road closures, or to, at least, mitigate the impact for those of us that live in the affected area. Thank you for taking the time to read my comments. I am happy to discuss this further if needed. Lisa J. Remal

subject: Road Closures at Temple Square for 2027
comment: I saw that the projected number of visitors for the 2027 Temple Square Open House, in practical terms, equates to a *maximum* of ~3,000 visitors per hour. This is spread across more than 40 acres. That comes directly from the Executive Director of the Downtown Alliance, Dee Brewer. Is 3,000 people per hour enough to justify closing two major downtown through-streets, each measuring ~90' x 660'? From everything I have seen, there will be no extra on-street programming or usage of the street-space, as our experience has been with the Mayor's annual Open Streets program on Main. There are also no SLC businesses on these blocks, to benefit from a pedestrianized zone... Most visitors will instead spend their time inside the block interiors, off the streets, within the existing Temple Square (which already includes overbuilt 12'-14' security walls). I'll ask again: is such a major inconvenience, the closing of these streets, justified for an entire half year? Perhaps instead of closing Temple streets, we should move our Open Streets on Main to the spring months of 2027 and align with this Temple celebration—this could keep the Temple streets open to through traffic, but encourage all our new visitors to continue their downtown experience along Main and encourage them to patronize our businesses. One last time: the estimate is only ~3,000 visitors per hour, maximum, spread across more than 40 acres of D-1 downtown space. comment: Dear City Council Members, The pond in Sugar House Park is a popular recreational feature, but in the event of a flood, it is a major retention basin in Salt Lake City's flood plan. The State Flood Zone map indicates that all of the Park property is in the Parley's Creek flood zone area. The map does not designate the private land being proposed for development, but major flood events have never made allowances for private property. Floods have always threatened the Sugar Business District. In 2005, water flows through SH Park reached 200 cubic feet per second. Major flooding occurred here in 1922, 1952, 1956,1983, and 2017. When sewer and water lines reached capacity, excess water was diverted to nearby streets or properties using sandbags to construct temporary water channels. Debris swept up by floodwater blocked segments of the creek, forcing the water to flow onto private property. Despite the diligent efforts of City and County engineers and public officials, no one can foresee events like cloudbursts and flashfloods (1952). Despite the optimism of the Magnus developers, it is foolish to deny that Sugar House Park is, first-and-foremost, a flood detention basin. Respectfully, Lynne Olson

subject: ICE detention shift to focus on more local solutions
comment: To Salt Lake City Council Members, I am writing to share my perspective regarding the city's current approach to immigration enforcement, particularly the decision to engage federal agencies at the local level. I want to begin by acknowledging that I have, in the past, supported the enforcement of immigration laws, including the deportation of undocumented individuals. I believe that laws exist for a reason and should be upheld. However, my support has always been rooted in a belief in balanced, fair, and community-conscious enforcement. It is for that reason that I feel compelled to express concern about the current tactic of involving federal agencies in what I believe are matters that can and should be handled by our local institutions. Our local law enforcement agencies are capable, accountable to our community, and better positioned to carry out their responsibilities with an understanding of the people they serve. Beyond concerns about jurisdiction and efficiency, I am also troubled by the financial implications of this approach. The cost of hiring or coordinating with federal agencies places an additional burden on our city's resources—funds that could otherwise be directed toward community programs, infrastructure, or public safety initiatives that more directly benefit residents. Equally important is the cultural impact of these decisions. Our city has long prided itself on being a place of friendliness, openness, and acceptance. Policies and actions that create fear or division within our community run counter to those values. Even when enforcement is necessary, it should be carried out in a way that reflects who we are as a city—measured, respectful, and mindful of the broader social fabric. I urge the Council to reconsider the current approach and to prioritize solutions that rely on our local agencies, uphold the law, and remain aligned with our community's values. We can maintain both order and compassion, and I believe our city is strongest when we do both. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Brigitte Bebey, Utah Resident

subject: Action against ICE Detention center

The acquisition of a warehouse in Salt Lake City to be converted into an ICE detention facility is an affront to the values of this community, and I expect you — as my elected representative — to do everything in your power to stop it. This is not abstract policy. This is a mass detention facility being built in our city, in our neighborhoods. Salt Lake City is a community built on the labor, culture, and contributions of immigrants. A detention facility of this scale does not make us safer — it makes us complicit in a system that has repeatedly been documented for its inhumane conditions, lack of medical care, family separation, and due process violations. I want to know, explicitly and on the record: What are YOU doing to stop this? Are you coordinating with the mayor's office? Are you exploring every legal, legislative, and regulatory tool available to block or delay this facility? Are you consulting with civil rights attorneys and immigration advocates? If not — why not? Your silence or inaction on this issue will not be forgotten. The residents of Salt Lake City are watching. We will remember who stood up and who stood aside when it mattered. subject: March 24 City Council Meeting / Statement of Support for Ruff Haven Crisis Sheltering Housing Funding Application
comment: Subject: Statement of Support for Ruff Haven Crisis Sheltering Housing Funding Application March 24th, 2026, Salt Lake City Council Hearing Dear Salt Lake City Council Members, I am writing to express my strong support for Ruff Haven Crisis Sheltering and their proposed outreach project serving unhoused individuals with companion animals in our community. As the Executive Director of the nonprofit Tailwinds Rental Assistance-dedicated to keeping people and their pets together by reducing barriers to pet-inclusive housing- particularly through assistance with pet deposits and pet fees - I have had the privilege of getting to know Ruff Haven's leadership team over the past three years. During that time, I have watched their impact in the Salt Lake community grow in both scale and effectiveness. They have become a trusted and influential voice in addressing the critical intersection of housing instability and pet ownership—and their work, in fact, directly inspired the creation and mission of Tailwinds. It is essential that our community recognize what national data clearly demonstrates: companion animals are not a barrier to stability, but a vital lifeline. For many individuals experiencing housing insecurity, pets provide emotional support, safety, and a sense of purpose. Any effort to address affordable housing or homelessness that does not account for companion animals risks falling short of meaningful, lasting impact. Ruff Haven's street outreach model reflects what we know to be the gold standard in serving vulnerable populations—meeting people where they are, building trust through person-to-person engagement, and connecting them to resources in a way that is both compassionate and practical. Their targeted outreach to individuals with pets is not only innovative, but necessary, particularly given that many remain unaware of evolving pet-inclusive shelter options. I can personally attest to the strength of Ruff Haven's leadership. They are courageous, strategic, and deeply committed to serving this often-overlooked population with dignity and care. Their ability to rapidly expand their reach while maintaining thoughtful, high-quality programming speaks to both their capability and their integrity. I strongly urge you to consider funding this outreach initiative. Investments in programs like Ruff Haven's do more than address immediate needs—they create pathways to stable housing, strengthen community trust, and reflect the compassion and forward-thinking values of Salt Lake City. It is difficult to imagine a more impactful use of resources in advancing both housing solutions and humane care. Thank you for your consideration and for your continued commitment to our community. Sincerely, Andrea Schaefer Executive Director Tailwinds Rental Assistance

subject: PLNPCM2025-00622, PLNPCM2025-00624
comment: Re: General Plan Amendment and Zoning Map Amendment for Sugar House Hotel Parcel Not generated by A.I. The massive Mixed Use Zoning Consolidation has just recently been enacted. The Planning Department up-zoned and increased the density potential for the Sugar House Business District ( SHBD ). It is therefore noteworthy that the proper zoning for this parcel, which abuts Sugar House Park (SHP ), was deliberately designated as MU-3. The proposed re-zone does not preserve open space and critical environmental areas. It does not accommodate and promote an increase in Salt Lake City's population. It does not protect water quality and supply by protecting ground water sources. To the contrary, it puts these fragile resources in danger. This re-zone does not identify, preserve and enhance view corridors and vistas, including views of natural lands around and within the City. This re-zone does not support and encourage architecture, development and infrastructure that is people focused and responsive to its surrounding context to enhance the public realm. In fact, it does the opposite. The Sugar House Master Plan ( SHMP ) does not, in any way, contemplate expansion of the Business District east of 1300 East. In fact, it very clearly excludes the area east of 1300 East from the Business District and emphasizes the parcel is considered on the periphery of the Business District. The SHMP values maintaining its historic character and encourages compatible development. The SHMP states the Town Center Scale should be centered around Monument Plaza and ends at the west side of 1300 East. Monument Plaza is considered the Gateway to Sugar House, not this parcel. The Community Benefits identified as pertaining to this project to support the re-zone are B - providing commercial space for local businesses and F - expanding public infrastructure that expands capacity for future development. For B the project proposes providing 25% below market rent for 3500 sq. ft., to be divided into 2 spaces, as well as an interest free loan for build out. Free space for community use, without free or reserved garage parking. A Greenbike station on Sugar House Park property. Public use of underground parking, which will not be free or reserved. 50 proposed FTE jobs ( this is misleading as most will be part time with no benefits, as is customary in the industry ). Except for the space for local businesses, none of these should be considered as meeting Community Benefit B. It is also a problematic conclusion that local eateries will welcome more competition from the hotel facilities. For F the project proposes that the hotel will provide 24 security for Sugar House Park. However, Sugar House Park is not a 24 hour destination and trying to make it one or an adjunct to this project is contrary to the use and purpose of the Park. Also that the public will have use of the garage. It also posits that the cost of the garage is a future expansion of public infrastructure. It also touts integrated Park improvements, which are clearly not future infrastructure expansions. None of these can realistically be considered as meeting section F. Other assertions are that the project will compete with AIRBNBs. It will not. While it is nice to believe that most of the hotel patrons will arrive with and use public transit while at the hotel, this is naive. While Sugar House is a great place to live, it is not a destination. Most visitors will go skiing or downtown. Since public transit does not run late enough for people to return in the evening, use of public transit is not practical. The General Plan Amendment and Zoning Map Amendment will stay with the parcel, not with the project. Therefore, any use allowed in MU-8 would be possible, whether suitable for a parcel which abuts a park or not. For all of the above reasons, the General Plan Amendment and Zoning Map Amendment should both be denied as inappropriate for this parcel and MU-3 should continue to be the proper zone.

comment: Good Evening Paul Zuckerman Salt Lake homeowner Graduate Degree in Park and Recreation Management I oppose changing the rezoning of this parcel. At an earlier council meeting, a developer was proposing a new condo to be built on the corner of 13th South and State Street. It would represent a welcomed upgrade to the aging, underutilized existing strip mall. Rightly so, council members took the time to ask if the building would be no more than 2 or 3 stories in height, presumably to fit with surrounding businesses, if it would provide ample set-back from the sidewalk and if trees would be planted. It was also requested that the featureless side of the building facing State Street could be redesigned to be more visually appealing. In short, would it fit. There seems to be no such concern regarding the placement of a proposed 7-9 story hotel on less than an acre of land with four public facing elevations. Judging by artist renderings, it would necessitate a hotel be built with little attention to those same aforementioned concerns. subject: ICE detention Facility
comment: Dear Council Members, I am writing as a concerned resident to strongly oppose the establishment of an ICE detention facility in Salt Lake County. I believe that facilities of this nature raise serious humanitarian concerns. Across the country, immigration detention centers have been widely criticized for unsafe conditions, lack of adequate medical care, and the emotional and physical toll they take on individuals and families. Bringing such a facility into our community does not reflect the values of compassion, dignity, and responsible governance that Salt Lake City strives to uphold. Beyond the moral concerns, I am troubled by the long-term impact this decision could have on our city's reputation. Approving a detention center risks associating Salt Lake City with policies and practices that many residents find deeply troubling. This could leave a lasting negative mark on our community. I would also urge the Council to reconsider how public or private resources are being allocated in this effort. If those same funds were directed toward humane and constructive solutions—such as legal assistance, community-based case management, or support for voluntary relocation—our city could be a part of a more effective and compassionate approach to immigration challenges. I respectfully ask that you reject any proposal that would allow an ICE detention facility to be established in our county. I hope you will stand with the many residents who want Salt Lake City to lead with humanity, fairness, and integrity. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Mindy Gautreau Resident of Cottonwood Heights

subject: Formal Suggestion: Noise Control for Vehicle Exhaust on 600 S & State St (Downtown)
comment: Dear Mayor Mendenhall, I am a resident of REDACTED, Salt Lake City, UT 84111. I am writing to share a formal suggestion regarding the excessive and disruptive noise caused by vehicles and motorcycles with modified exhausts and resonators. While I understand that living downtown involves urban activity, the frequent, high-decibel noise from these modified vehicles is a direct violation of City Ordinance 9.28.060. Specifically, the intersection of 600 South and State Street has become an unbearable hotspot. State Street is consistently the loudest area, acting as a corridor where drivers accelerate with loud resonators, particularly late at night. I would like to emphasize that this is not just an inconvenience; it is a health and safety issue for our families. We have a baby at home, and there are many other children living in this building whose sleep and well-being are constantly disrupted by these illegal exhausts. To address this, I propose the following solutions: • Implementation of "Noise Cameras": I suggest Salt Lake City look into the pilot programs used in New York City, which utilize sound-activated enforcement cameras to automatically ticket vehicles that exceed legal decibel limits. This technology would provide consistent enforcement at loud intersections like 600 S and State St. • Residential "Quiet Zone" Signage: I recommend installing official "Quiet Zone" signs along 600 South and State Street to remind drivers that they are passing through a high-density residential area where children and families live. • Targeted Enforcement: Increased patrols by SLCPD specifically focused on equipment violations (modified mufflers/resonators) during peak nighttime hours at the State Street entry points to the city. As Downtown continues to grow with more families moving into residential units like 600 Lofts, it is vital that we balance urban vibrancy with a livable, quiet environment for our children. Thank you for your time and for your dedication to making Salt Lake City a better place for all residents. Best regards, Mario Palacios

comment: Hello, I plan to make a public comment at tomorrow's meeting and wanted to share my remarks in advance: My name is Breanne Clement, and I live in District 7. subject: Proposed Rezone at 2111S, 1300 E. for Proposed Sugar House Park Hotel
comment: Members of the Salt Lake City Council, I'm writing to ask that you deny the proposed rezone for the proposed Sugar House Park Hotel. As a Salt Lake City resident and a developer myself, I want to clarify that I'm not a NIMBY, who is anti-development. Developments are a necessary part of our city and they are needed to accommodate the city's growing population and the community's ever-changing needs. But we need to advocate for smart development. New projects need to be constructed in a way that adds value to the residents and that doesn't detract from the community. Sugarhouse Park is a gem in our city. As a critical space for our community, we need to protect it. A seven-story structure would be overbearing on that parcel. After reviewing the submitted drawings, As a developer myself, I'm skeptical at the ability of the parcel to handle adequate parking and traffic circulation. I'm concerned the flow of traffic and parking for the proposed development will be detrimental to the park and will make it unsafe for runners, cyclists, and other park users who go to Sugarhouse Park to specifically get away from traffic. Some of the plans even show a road connecting the hotel parking lot to the Sugarhouse Park Road. While a road connecting the hotel parking lot to the Park Road would be catastrophic to the park, even completely separate access that is limited to 21st South and /or 13th East would degrade the park experience. The parcel is small enough that traffic and parking will inevitably spill into the park and create more traffic. Members of the community do not want The Park to turn into the circulation road and parking lot for a hotel. This will make the park unsafe for the residents who specifically utilize the park as a place to recreate away from traffic. In addition, this rezone sets a dangerous precedent for future development. It's clear that the developers paid too much for this property and now they are relying on the city council to approve this rezone so they can achieve their desired returns. By approving this rezone, the council will be justifying the inflated price. This means brokers and land sellers are going to demand higher prices in the area, which makes future development in the Sugarhouse area even more difficult. With housing prices being at an all-time high in our city, higher land prices will make affordable housing projects even less achievable for other developers. If Magnus wants to develop this site, there is no reason why they can't work within the current zoning regulations. There's no need for them to go above the current 40' maximum height limit, other than to improve their financial situation. Increasing the height for a hotel use does not benefit the local community, but it will generate more traffic in and around the Park, which hurts everyone. Whatever is developed on this corner should be a low-impact use that won't have any negative impact on the park. As you prepare to vote on this item, I would implore you to deny this rezone and ensure that The Park stays a beautiful, safe, and low-traffic place for Salt Lake Residents to enjoy. Let's set a precedent for smart development. Let's advocate for density in the right locations, for uses that benefit the community, such as affordable housing. And let's set a precedent to preserve community space and not allow commercially-driven developments with little community benefit to devalue and encroach on these areas. Signed, Kye Nielsen A Sugarhouse Resident and a developer
